Contracts · open anywhere

Days 1 to 4 · recap

Who does what: the actor formula
Who + must/may/will + what + when. Name the person who acts, then the verb.
must / may / will vs shall
must = duty · must not = ban · may = right · will = a future step of a procedure · shall is doubtful.
Cut the waste
Doublets, bloat and old words. Keep words that carry meaning (“prior”, “written”).
Negatives and passive
Avoid stacked “not”. Name the actor for duties, rights and consequences.
Time words and vague standards
“forthwith”, “promptly”, “reasonable” → a number of days or an objective test.
Formulas: royalty and Net Revenue
Define each term; say who calculates, when, and from which figures.
Conditionals
IF · WHEN · UNLESS · PROVIDED THAT · SUBJECT TO: when does the duty switch on, and who decides?
Boilerplate
Entire agreement, amendment, assignment, notices, governing law, dispute resolution, severability, waiver…
Purpose and forms
Advise, inform, persuade. Email, letter, memo. Four steps: mind map, blueprint, construct, inspect.
Polite and direct
would / could / if; negative, indirect and tag questions.
Anatomy of an agreement
Nine elements: recitals, definitions, conditions precedent, agreements, warranties, boilerplate, schedules, signatures, appendices.
Clause Lab
Mark, organise, redraft. Keep prior/written/consent: cut waste, not content.
Knock-for-knock
Each partner bears the losses of its own people and property (D2 Article 5).

Introduction · why each document exists

INTRODUCTION

Read first (8 minutes). Before we review the documents, ask what each pair of parties wanted when it signed. A contract is the written form of an intention. When two documents seem to say different things, it helps to remember what each was made for.

A. Contract types: the Horizon family

TRANSITION

"Before we look inside any contract, we ask a simpler question: what kind of contract is it? A contract type answers one question: what job does this document do? Here are five extracts. Do not read them all: read the first line and decide."

Before we start · what is an agreement?

“A well-drafted contract is understandable by the employee who inherited it five years after it was struck and knew nothing of the initial negotiations.” (Craig Kaiser, attorney)

A contract is a formal agreement between people or businesses. Whenever we make one, we create a legal relationship.

Key aspects of every contract: intent (the parties mean to be bound), offer (a definite promise), acceptance (an unequivocal statement; it may take effect when the accepting party posts it) and consideration (usually money, but it can be an exchange of services or goods). Question: is an invitation to treat (a shop window, a tender call, an auction) an offer? Not by itself: it invites others to make offers.

Types. Each type of agreement has its standard form. The main difference is between business-to-business (B2B) and business-to-consumer (B2C) agreements: B2C contracts get extra protection from the law.

Aim of an agreement. It is a permanent record that clarifies the rights and obligations of the parties. So it must be clear and not confusing: plain English makes it easy to understand and interpret. That is why we pay attention to terminology, clauses and punctuation.

SAY · FEEDBACK

Feedback (3 minutes). "Which type was easiest? Which was the hardest?" Usually the joint venture against the framework: both organise work between companies. The difference: the JV shares risk and results; the framework only sets rules for future orders.

Name the key sign of each type: NDA = "Confidential Information"; JV = "Operator", "cash calls"; licence = "grant of rights"; framework = "Call-Off"; letter = "formal notice".

POSSIBLE QUESTIONS · ANSWERS

Q: Is a "framework" a contract to buy? A: No. It sets the rules for future orders. The purchase happens in each Call-Off (D3 clause 4). That is why D3 says it creates no minimum volume.

Q: Is Annex I a separate contract? A: It is a separate document but not a separate contract: it is an integral part of D2. That is why D2 15.3 and Annex I H.2 must agree on which one prevails.

Case 1The comma that cost millions8 minLETTER · D4

A short case about one humble comma. Look at the picture, read, follow the guide, predict, and only then reveal how the court resolved it.

Part of the contractLanguage of the whole contract
Clause / headingPunctuation in any list (the Oxford, or serial, comma)
Why it mattersA comma can decide who is paid, who is exempt and who pays. Contracts are read as written.
What is the difference between “The lawyer said the judge was a fool” and “The lawyer, said the judge, was a fool”?
✗ Read both slowly: who is speaking?
✗ In the first sentence the lawyer is speaking.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✓ The commas turn the speaker into the subject: in the second sentence the judge is the speaker and the lawyer is the fool.

The case · overtime for the drivers (Maine, USA)

The law

Overtime is not due for workers involved in: “the canning, processing, preserving, freezing, drying, marketing, storing, packing for shipment or distribution of: (1) agricultural produce; (2) meat and fish products; and (3) perishable foods.”

Note: there is no comma after “shipment” and before “or distribution”. Some drivers who only distribute perishable foods say they are owed overtime.

Follow the reading · before the answer
  1. Read the list of activities. Count them: how many are there, and which verbs or nouns are they?
  2. Look at the last item: “packing for shipment or distribution of”. Is it one activity (packing for shipment, or for distribution) or two (packing for shipment; and distribution)?
  3. Take the drivers’ side: which reading gives them overtime? Take the dairy’s side: which reading exempts them?
  4. Ask what a comma after “shipment” would have changed. Then write your prediction: who wins, and why?
How the court resolved it. The US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit (O’Connor v. Oakhurst Dairy, 2017) found the exemption genuinely ambiguous. The overtime law protects workers, so the court read the ambiguity in the workers’ favour: “distribution” alone was not exempt, and the drivers were owed overtime. The case later settled for USD 5 million, and the law was rewritten (verify). Lesson: one missing comma turned a list of activities into an argument; a clearer list (with “and/or”, a serial comma, or bullet points (a), (b), (c)) would have avoided it.
TEACHER NOTE · Case 1

Instructor note. “Oxford comma” = the comma before “and/or” in a list of three or more. It is not the only issue: ask “From your experience, what other errors may occur besides punctuation?” (wrong cross-references, undefined terms, two names for one thing, numbers that differ in words and figures). Link: D2 2.1 cites “Article 7” for force majeure, which is in fact Article 6: a cross-reference error with the same effect as a comma.

Time. About 6 minutes; the answer appears only when the participant presses the button. The facts come from the First Circuit decision and press reports (verify).

B. Elements of an agreement

TRANSITION

"Every agreement is built from the same nine parts: recitals, definitions, conditions precedent, agreements, representations and warranties, boilerplate, schedules, signatures and appendices. We saw them on the NDA. Today we use them to read three contracts we have not read: D2, Annex I and D3. First, an ID card."

The NDA "must have" list (from your reference sheet) · model for today's ID cards

1 Parties · 2 Term · 3 Definition of Confidential Information and its use · 4 Obligations of the parties · 5 Exceptions · 6 Consequences of breach · 7 Right to seek an injunction · 8 Jurisdiction and governing law · 9 Dispute resolution · 10 Return of Confidential Information.

Each must-have has three parts: what it must contain, a note, an example. Today you build the same card for a new contract. Typical durations such as 3 to 5 years come from general guides (verify).

Terms and conditions

Terms and conditions are the promises that both parties agree to be bound by. They may be express (written) or implied (the law adds them). In the UK, contracts for the sale of goods are governed by the Sale of Goods Act; in the US, by the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC).

① Pick a tool. ② Click words, or drag across them. Click again with the same tool to undo. Everyone works differently: there is no single right way to mark.

PARTIES · GER (Operator, 60%) and PETROX (Non-Operator, 40%) · effective 30 June 2025 · the preamble gives GER four names (Operator, GER, the Licensor, First Party)
PartiesPARTIESwho makes the promises, and what each one is called

Why it matters. It names who is bound. A wrong or inconsistent name (GER has four) makes later clauses unclear about who must do what.

Why so many names for GER? The preamble calls GER “Operator”, “GER”, “the Licensor” and “First Party”, and PETROX “Non-Operator”, “PETROX”, “the Licensee” and “Second Party”. The drafter wanted to show roles (who runs the work, who grants the licence), but four names for one company make the reader ask every time: “is this the same company?”. Plain-English rule: one name for one person, defined once.

The correct way to address GER, contract by contract. D2: “GER” everywhere, and “GER, as Operator” only when the role matters (Articles 7 and 8); PETROX is “PETROX”, or “PETROX, as Licensee” in the licence articles. Annex I: “GER” and “PETROX” (the Annex calls PETROX “Receiving Party”, an NDA word that is not defined there). D3: “GER” (acting as Operator under the JDA, clause 1) and “the Contractor” for Meridian. NDA (D1): “GER” and “PETROX”, with “Disclosing Party” and “Receiving Party” used only as roles.

Careful: “Licensor” means GER in D2, but in D3 Schedule 1 it means Helix Process Technologies. The same word with two meanings in one project is a trap: do not reuse a defined word across documents.

ARTICLE 1 Definitions · Joint Account, Joint Operations, Licensed Technology (SeismoCore 7.2), Contract Area (Blocks 14/06 and 15/07), Participating Interest · the Work Programme is said to be approved under Article 6
Article 1 · DefinitionsDICTIONARYwhat the capitalised words mean

Why it matters. Every capitalised word later in the contract takes its meaning from here. A weak definition quietly changes the rights of the parties.

Every word that starts with a capital letter in the contract (Joint Account, Contract Area, Operator…) has its meaning fixed here. Read this article first, then look for two things: words used later that are not defined (“Gross Revenue” appears in Article 3 and Schedule 3 and is never defined) and wrong numbers.

Example of a wrong number: “Joint Operations” says the Work Programme is approved “in accordance with Article 6”, but the Work Programme is Article 7 (Article 6 is Force Majeure). A wrong number sends the reader to the wrong rule.

ARTICLE 2 Grant of licence · a non-exclusive, non-transferable licence to use SeismoCore, only inside the Contract Area · conditional on payment and no default · "save where Article 7 (Force Majeure) applies"
Article 2 · Grant of licencePERMISSIONwhat PETROX may do with the software, and where

Why it matters. It is the legal permission to use the software. Without it PETROX would infringe GER’s rights; its limits (where, by whom, on what conditions) are the limits of the licence.

The key words. Non-exclusive: GER may license the software to others too. Non-transferable: PETROX cannot pass the licence to anyone else. Non-sublicensable: PETROX cannot give sub-licences. PETROX may use the software only inside the Contract Area and only for three jobs: processing, modelling and reservoir characterisation.

What does “save where Article 7 (Force Majeure) applies” mean? “Save” is an old word for “except”. The licence is given on conditions: PETROX must have paid what it owes and there must be no Event of Default, except where force majeure applies. In plain words: if something outside PETROX’s control (for example a bank strike) stops a payment, the licence should not be lost for that reason.

Two problems. (1) Wrong reference: force majeure is Article 6; Article 7 is the Work Programme. (2) Unclear effect: does the exception pause the conditions or cancel them, and for how long? Plain version: “The licence is granted on condition that PETROX pays all amounts due and that no Event of Default is continuing, unless Article 6 (Force Majeure) applies.” Write “except” or “unless”, never “save”.

ARTICLE 3 Royalty · PETROX pays GER 3.5% of Net Revenue · deductions capped at 20% of Gross Revenue · multiplier in "Schedule 3, Part B, Column 4" · GER may change it on 60 days’ notice · audit once a year, cost decided by the Operator
Article 3 · RoyaltyPRICEwhat PETROX pays for the software

Why it matters. It is the price. Every unclear word here (Net or Gross Revenue, deductions, multiplier) is money in dispute.

Royalty. A payment for the right to use someone else’s property, here GER’s software. Instead of one fixed fee, PETROX pays a percentage (3.5%) of what it earns from the wells where it used the software. The more it earns, the more it pays.

Gross Revenue is all the money PETROX receives from selling the oil and gas, before taking anything off. Net Revenue is what is left after the deductions the contract allows. The 3.5% is calculated on the Net figure.

“Deductions capped at 20% of Gross Revenue”. PETROX may subtract some costs (third-party costs of using the software), but never more than 20% of the gross figure. Invented example: gross 20 million, so at most 4 million may be subtracted, even if the costs were 5 million; Net Revenue is then at least 16 million.

The multiplier. A number that moves the royalty up or down with production volume (1.15 means 15% more). It is said to be in “Schedule 3, Part B, Column 4”, but that Part is only the reporting calendar: the table does not exist. GER may change it on 60 days’ notice, yet 15.2 says any amendment needs both signatures.

Audit. GER may check PETROX’s books once a year (5 Business Days’ notice) to verify the royalty. Differences under 2% are ignored. The cost goes to “the party that bears the greater burden”, and the Operator decides who that is. The Operator is GER: one of the parties acts as the judge.

ARTICLE 4 Intellectual property and data · GER keeps the intellectual property in SeismoCore · Derived Data owned "in equal undivided shares, subject to" three different splits: 60/40, 50/50, 70/30
Article 4 · Intellectual property and dataOWNERSHIPwho owns the software and what is created with it

Why it matters. Value of the project: the software stays with GER, and the data PETROX creates must have a clear owner and clear shares.

Intellectual property (IP) means things you own but cannot touch: software, inventions, know-how. 4.1: GER keeps all the IP in SeismoCore. 4.2: “Derived Data” is what PETROX creates while using it.

The problem. 4.2 says “equal undivided shares” (equal means 50/50) and then, “subject to” three different splits: 60/40, 50/50 and 70/30. A new method for modelling a reservoir fits two categories (modelling and “New IP”). So what share does PETROX own? We work on this in Ex 5.13.

ARTICLE 5 Knock-for-knock · each party covers injury to its own people and damage to its own property, even if the other party was negligent · 5.2: PETROX covers injury to GER’s people "howsoever caused"
Article 5 · Knock-for-knockOWN LOSSeach side bears the loss of its own people and property

Why it matters. It decides who carries the loss of injury and damage. A one-sided sentence (5.2) can silently change the commercial deal.

Knock-for-knock in general terms. Each company carries the losses of its own people and its own property, whoever caused the accident. Everyday picture: two neighbours agree that each one pays for the repair of their own car, without arguing about who was at fault.

Why oil and gas uses it. Offshore accidents involve many companies, and arguing about fault can take years. With knock-for-knock each company insures its own people and equipment and nobody sues anybody.

In D2. 5.1 is two-way. 5.2 breaks the symmetry: PETROX covers injury to GER’s people “howsoever caused”. Which clause is the deal? (Ex 5.9). Also, 5.1 reaches gross negligence: whether that is allowed depends on the governing law (verify).

ARTICLE 6 Force majeure · relief to the extent performance is prevented · notice "as soon as reasonably practicable" · no time limit and nothing on payments
Article 6 · Force majeureEXCUSEwhat happens when something outside our control stops us

Why it matters. It says who is excused when something outside control happens. Without a notice date, a payment rule and a long-stop, both sides are exposed.

Force majeure means events beyond anyone’s control (war, flood, earthquake…). A party that cannot perform because of them is excused for as long as the event prevents it.

Is “as soon as reasonably practicable” ambiguous? Yes. “Reasonably” and “practicable” are judgement words: one side says 40 days was practicable, the other says it was not, and the clause gives no date to settle it.

How to tighten it. (1) A number: “within 5 Business Days after the event begins” (the course standard in Ex 5.14 uses 48 hours; any number is a negotiation). (2) What the notice must contain: the event, the obligations affected and the expected duration. (3) The consequence: if the notice is late, relief starts only from the day of the notice. (4) A long-stop: if the event lasts 90 or 180 days, either party may end the agreement (D3 clause 21 uses 90 days). (5) Payments already due are not excused (D3 clause 21 says so). Also: the definition is not numbered (6.1).

ARTICLE 7 Work programme and budget · Operating Committee, two representatives each · decisions need 65% of the interests · Operator proposes by 1 October · may overspend up to 10%
Article 7 · Work programme and budgetPLANthe yearly work and budget, and how the committee votes

Why it matters. It controls the yearly plan, the budget and how decisions are taken: it decides who has the real power in the joint venture.

Each year GER, as Operator, proposes the work and the budget; the Operating Committee approves it. Decisions need 65% of the interests: with 60/40, neither GER (60%) nor PETROX (40%) can decide alone, so both must agree on every decision. The clause does not say what happens if they cannot agree (a deadlock).

7.3 lets GER overspend by 10% without approval. This matters for D3: the EUR 42,000,000 Call-Off is charged to the Joint Account.

ARTICLE 8 Operatorship, Joint Account and cash calls · GER operates diligently and keeps the Joint Account in USD; monthly cash calls, each party pays its share within 20 days · late interest SOFR + 3 points
Article 8 · Operatorship, Joint Account and cash callsMANAGERGER runs the work and asks for the money (cash calls)

Why it matters. It is how the money moves: GER runs the work and the partners fund it. Late funding has interest and can lead to default.

What is a cash call? In a joint venture the Operator (GER) pays the bills first (drilling, equipment, staff). Every month it sends the partners a cash call: a request for their share of the money needed. PETROX has 40%, so it pays 40% of the costs. Think of it as an advance invoice for your share of the costs. Invented example: costs of USD 1,000,000 in the month; PETROX pays USD 400,000 within 20 days of receiving the cash call.

What does “late interest SOFR + 3” mean? If PETROX pays late, it owes interest. SOFR is the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, a benchmark interest rate for US dollars published daily by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. “+ 3 points” means three percentage points more. Invented example: if SOFR were 4%, late payments would bear 7% a year.

A clear clause also says which SOFR (which day, or an average), that the rate is yearly, and what happens if SOFR stops being published.

ARTICLE 9 Representations and warranties · authority to sign · GER has the right to license · no promise that the software is error-free · anti-bribery
Article 9 · Representations and warrantiesTRUTHstatements each side says are true today

Why it matters. Statements that each side says are true today. If they are false the other side has a claim; if they are missing it has nothing to rely on.

A representation or warranty is a statement of fact that a party says is true today: we have authority to sign; GER has the right to license the software; we follow anti-bribery laws. If the statement is false, that party is in breach. Notice what GER does not promise: that the software is error-free or fit for any purpose.

ARTICLE 10 Limitation of liability · no indirect loss or lost profit · cap of USD 25,000,000 per party (not for cash calls, royalties or Article 5) · no limit for fraud or wilful misconduct
Article 10 · Limitation of liabilityLIMITthe most anyone can lose or pay if something goes wrong

Why it matters. It tells each side how much it can lose. A cap that conflicts with another clause or document creates a gap nobody planned.

10.1 Neither party pays the other for indirect or consequential loss or for lost production, profit or revenue. Example: if GER’s software fails and PETROX’s well starts producing late, PETROX cannot claim the profit it would have made.

10.2 There is a ceiling: for everything under D2 and Annex I, each party can be made to pay at most USD 25,000,000. Exceptions with no ceiling: cash calls, royalties and the Article 5 indemnities (you must always pay what you owe).

10.3 The ceiling and the exclusions do not protect fraud or wilful misconduct: a party that cheats on purpose pays everything.

Why it matters. The cap tells each side its maximum risk and how much insurance to buy. Watch: 10.3 does not mention gross negligence, and Annex I G.1 sets another ceiling for GER (royalties of the last 12 months): see Ex 5.9.

ARTICLE 11 Events of default and termination · a material breach not cured within 30 days after formal notice is an Event of Default; then termination with immediate effect · 11.2 lists what the notice must say
Article 11 · Events of default and terminationEXITwhen and how the deal can end

Why it matters. It tells you how the deal ends and what must be done first (notice, cure period). If the notice does not follow 11.2 the clock does not start.

An Event of Default is a serious breach that has not been put right in time. After a formal written notice, the party in breach has 30 days to cure (fix) it. 11.2 says what the notice must contain: that it is a notice under 11.2, which provision was breached, the facts and the cure period. Only after the cure period can the other party end the contract with immediate effect (11.3). This is the procedure the D4 letter should follow (Ex 5.11).

ARTICLE 12 Assignment · consent needed to transfer the contract · a change of control of PETROX needs GER’s consent
Article 12 · AssignmentNO SWAPPINGyou cannot hand the contract to someone else without consent

Why it matters. It protects the choice of partner: nobody can swap the other party, even by a change of control, without consent.

Assignment is handing your rights or duties to someone else. Neither party may do it without the other’s written consent (which cannot be unreasonably withheld). If PETROX is taken over (a change of control), GER must consent: GER decides who its partner is.

ARTICLE 13 Governing law and disputes · English law; ICC arbitration in London, three arbitrators · urgent court relief allowed
Article 13 · Governing law and disputesREFEREEwhich law applies and who decides a dispute

Why it matters. It chooses the law and who decides a dispute. All other clauses will be read through this one.

Law and forum. English law applies. Disputes go to ICC arbitration: three private arbitrators, seat London, in English. An arbitration can take many months to set up.

What does “urgent court relief allowed” mean? Some harm cannot wait for the arbitrators. Example: PETROX is about to hand SeismoCore to a competitor tomorrow. 13.3 lets either party ask a court quickly for a temporary order (for example, an order to stop the disclosure) while the arbitration decides the real dispute. The court does not take the case away from the arbitrators. Disputes about the Joint Account may go to an independent accounting expert. (How and when a court can help an arbitration depends on the law of the seat: verify.)

ARTICLE 14 Notices · in writing, in English, by hand, courier or email · a notice under 11.2 must also go by courier · PETROX: the Company Secretary
Article 14 · NoticesPOSTBOXhow and where formal messages are sent

Why it matters. It decides whether a message has legally arrived. A notice sent the wrong way may be ignored by the court.

This article says how a formal message counts. A notice under 11.2 or of termination must also go by courier. PETROX’s notices go to the Company Secretary, GER’s to the Head of Legal Affairs. Receipt rules: by courier, the second Business Day after dispatch; by email, the next Business Day. A letter sent the wrong way may not start the cure clock (Ex 5.11).

ARTICLE 15 General provisions · entire agreement · amendments in writing signed by both · 15.3: if D2 and Annex I conflict on the licence, Annex I prevails
Article 15 · General provisionsSMALL PRINTstandard end clauses and which document wins

Why it matters. The end clauses decide which text wins in a conflict and how the contract can be changed. Gaps here make every other clause weaker.

Entire agreement: what is not written here does not count. Amendments: only in writing, signed by both (this clashes with GER changing the multiplier alone in 3.1).

Why is 15.3 ambiguous? It says that if D2 and Annex I conflict on the licence, Annex I prevails. Annex I H.2 says that if Annex I conflicts with D2, D2 prevails. Each document hands the win to the other, and the reader goes round in a circle: like two bosses each telling you “follow the other one’s instructions”.

It matters because licence rules differ: the liability cap is USD 25,000,000 in D2 10.2 but the royalties of the last 12 months in Annex I G.1. Fix: one rule in one place.

SCHEDULES · 1 Contract Area · 2 Accounting procedure · 3 Net Revenue: Permitted Deductions "are not subject to any percentage limit"
SchedulesMAPS AND RULES1 the area · 2 accounting rules · 3 money definitions

Why it matters. Schedules hold the numbers and the definitions the articles depend on. A schedule that contradicts an article creates a dispute.

Schedules are attachments that hold the details.

The ambiguity in Schedule 3. Article 3.1 says deductions are capped at 20% of Gross Revenue. Schedule 3, Part A says Permitted Deductions “are not subject to any percentage limit” and lists more kinds of deduction (transport and processing, taxes, the Operator’s overhead). Same subject, two answers. PETROX will say there is no limit (it subtracts more and pays less); GER will say 20%. D2 has no rule saying whether the body or the schedules win. And Gross Revenue is used but never defined.

SUGGESTED DRAFTING · plain English, same purpose. Use it as feedback on how you organised the clause.

ID card · D2 (JV). Parties: GER (Operator, 60%) and PETROX (Non-Operator, 40%). Purpose: to develop and produce together, with the SeismoCore licence attached as Annex I. Key duty: GER runs the Joint Operations and keeps the Joint Account (Art. 8). Money: royalty on Net Revenue (Art. 3); monthly cash calls, each Party pays its share within 20 days (8.3). Risk: knock-for-knock (Art. 5), no indirect loss (10.1), cap of USD 25,000,000 (10.2), force majeure (Art. 6). Exit: Event of Default after 30 days to cure (11.1), termination with immediate effect (11.3). Law: English law; ICC arbitration, seat London (Art. 13); notices in Art. 14.

X-ray 2 · Annex I Technology and Data Licence

Open it from the side table: . Same method.

Under each line you will find its one-word label and plain meaning. Press Explain ▾ for what to say.

① Pick a tool. ② Click words, or drag across them. Click again with the same tool to undo. Everyone works differently: there is no single right way to mark.

INTRODUCTION · part of D2, same effective date (30 June 2025) · GER licenses SeismoCore to PETROX · PETROX is called "Receiving Party" here
IntroductionATTACHMENTpart of D2, not a separate contract

Why it matters. It tells you that the licence is part of D2: they must be read together, and a conflict between them needs a rule.

Annex I forms an integral part of D2 (D2 Article 1): same Effective Date, and it ends with D2.

Names. In the Annex GER is the licensor and PETROX the licensee, but A.1 calls PETROX the “Receiving Party”, an NDA word that is not defined in the Annex. Correct way: “GER” and “PETROX” (or “PETROX, as Licensee”), exactly as in D2: one name each.

SECTION A Grant of rights · a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, revocable licence · only on the infrastructure in Schedule A-2 · only the people in Exhibit A-1 · to process the "Seismic Data"
Section A · Grant of rightsPERMISSIONwhat PETROX may do, with whom and where

Why it matters. It is the licence itself: what PETROX may do, with whom, where and for what. Anything outside the grant is a breach.

Limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, revocable. Limited: only for the uses listed. Non-exclusive: GER may license others. Non-transferable: PETROX cannot pass it on. Revocable: GER can withdraw it (see F.3).

“Seismic Data” is used here but is not defined: whose data? GER’s (the NDA Schedule 1 list)? PETROX’s? Both?

SECTION B Licence fees · tiers from 2.0% to 5.0% by "Annual Gross Revenue" (B.1) · but fees are "calculated on the basis of Net Revenue" (B.2)
Section B · Licence feesPRICEthe fee tiers

Why it matters. The fee for the software: if the tier base and the fee base are different measures, two people calculate two prices.

A tier table: the bigger PETROX’s revenue, the higher the rate (2.0% up to 5.0%) and the multiplier (0.85x to 1.30x).

Problem 1: the table is by “Annual Gross Revenue”, but B.2 says fees are calculated on Net Revenue: two measures. Problem 2: D2 Article 3 uses a flat 3.5%. Two price lists for the same licence; which one applies depends on which document prevails (15.3 or H.2), and that is circular.

SECTION C Confidentiality · the terms of the NDA of 14 February 2025 apply to PETROX’s use of the technology
Section C · ConfidentialitySECREThow the technology is kept confidential

Why it matters. It protects the technology: it brings in the NDA. If the NDA is shorter or narrower, the software is less protected than it looks.

C.1 says the terms of the NDA apply to PETROX’s use of the software. The NDA was written to let PETROX evaluate GER’s data; it lasted two years (until 14 February 2027) and its Schedule 1 lists data and models, not software. The licence runs until 2035. Software deserves its own confidentiality clause with its own duration. Note also that C.1 creates no new duty: it only points to the NDA.

SECTION D Support and updates · GER: remote support on Business Days, 09:00 to 17:00 Milan time · updates · up to 10 person-days of training
Section D · Support and updatesHELPsupport, updates and training

Why it matters. What PETROX gets besides the licence (support, updates, training). It limits GER’s service duty.

GER promises remote support in office hours, the updates released during the term and up to 10 person-days of training. The clause says “will provide”: in plain drafting a duty is written “must”. What is missing: response times, and what happens if support fails.

SECTION E Warranties · GER has the right to grant the licence · "as is": no promise that the software is error-free
Section E · WarrantiesAS-ISwhat GER does and does not promise

Why it matters. What GER promises about the software and, just as important, what it does not (as-is). It sets what PETROX can claim if it fails.

“As is” means GER hands the software over in its present state and does not promise that it is free from errors or fit for any purpose. The risk of relying on the outputs moves to PETROX. D2 9.2 says the same: the two documents agree.

SECTION F Term, suspension and termination · until the end of D2 or the 10th anniversary, whichever comes first · GER may suspend after 10 days of non-payment · GER may revoke on 30 days’ notice if it "determines" a security risk · copies returned or destroyed within 30 days
Section F · Term, suspension and terminationLIFEhow long the licence lasts and how it can be paused or ended

Why it matters. How long PETROX may use the software, and when GER can suspend or end the licence. It is the exit clause of the licence.

Suspend = temporarily stop access (F.2: after 10 days of non-payment). Revoke = cancel the licence (F.3: on 30 days’ notice if GER “determines” a security risk: GER decides alone).

This clashes with D2 Article 11, where a party can end the contract only after an Event of Default and a 30-day cure period. Also 10 days (F.2) against 30 days (D2 11.1(a)) for non-payment: two clocks. The licence ends with D2 or on 30 June 2035, whichever comes first.

SECTION G Liability · GER’s liability limited to the royalties PETROX paid in the previous 12 months · Article 10 of D2 also applies
Section G · LiabilityLIMITthe most GER can owe

Why it matters. The most GER can owe PETROX for software problems. It can differ from the cap in D2 Article 10.

G.1 says D2 Article 10 applies and adds a second ceiling: GER cannot owe more than the royalties PETROX paid in the 12 months before the claim. In the first year that may be a small sum, while D2 10.2 says USD 25,000,000. Which ceiling applies depends on which document prevails (see H.2).

SECTION H General · governed by the law and dispute rules of D2 · H.2: if Annex I and D2 conflict, the Agreement prevails · notices under D2 Article 14
Section H · GeneralSMALL PRINTlaw, which document wins, notices

Why it matters. Law, which document prevails and notices: the glue between Annex I and D2.

Law and disputes come from D2 (English law, ICC London). H.2 says the Agreement prevails over the Annex, while D2 15.3 says the Annex prevails on the licence: each document hands the win to the other (Ex 5.9). Notices go through D2 Article 14.

EXHIBIT A-1 · four named PETROX people authorised to use the software
Exhibit a-1NAMESwho may use the software

Why it matters. Names the people allowed to use the software: a person outside the list is a breach.

Only these four people may use the software. If one leaves, how is another added? The Annex does not say.

SCHEDULE A-2 · GER server in Milan, access by VPN, no installation or local storage anywhere else
Schedule a-2PLACEwhere the software may run

Why it matters. Says where the software may run (the approved infrastructure): using another server is a breach.

The software runs only on GER’s own server in Milan, reached by VPN. PETROX cannot install it or keep outputs locally: the software never leaves GER’s control.

SUGGESTED DRAFTING · plain English, same purpose. Use it as feedback on how you organised the clause.

ID card · Annex I (licence). Parties: GER (licensor) and PETROX (licensee). Purpose: to let PETROX use SeismoCore to process and model the seismic data in the Contract Area. Key duty: GER grants a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, revocable licence (A.1); PETROX uses it only on the approved infrastructure (Schedule A-2) and only through the people listed in Exhibit A-1. Money: fees by revenue tier (Section B). Risk: licence given "as is" (E.2); GER’s liability capped at the royalties paid in the previous 12 months (G.1). Exit: GER may suspend after 10 days of non-payment (F.2) or revoke on 30 days’ notice for a security risk (F.3); term up to 10 years (F.1). Law: the law and disputes rules of the JV (H.1); notices under JV Art. 14 (H.3).

Notice that Annex I has no law of its own: it borrows the JV’s. That is why it is an integral part of D2.

X-ray 3 · D3 Master Collaboration and Framework Agreement

Open it from the side table: . Same method.

Under each line you will find its one-word label and plain meaning. Press Explain ▾ for what to say.

① Pick a tool. ② Click words, or drag across them. Click again with the same tool to undo. Everyone works differently: there is no single right way to mark.

PARTIES · GER (as Operator of the JV) and Meridian Offshore Systems Ltd (Contractor) · effective 18 January 2027
PartiesPARTIESwho makes the promises, and what each one is called

Why it matters. It names who contracts. GER signs as Operator of the JV, so the cost reaches PETROX.

Names in D3. “GER” (acting as Operator under the JDA: clause 1) and “the Contractor” (Meridian). Use those two names only.

Careful: “Licensor” in D3 Schedule 1 means Helix Process Technologies, not GER; in D2 “the Licensor” is GER. The same word, two companies: avoid reusing defined words across documents.

Who pays? GER signs as Operator, but the cost falls on the Joint Account: PETROX pays 40% without signing.

1 Purpose and contracting model · a framework for supply, logistics and integration · the price of each Call-Off is charged to the Joint Account · no minimum volume, no exclusivity, no guaranteed award
Clause 1 · Purpose and contracting modelPURPOSEwhat the framework is for

Why it matters. It tells you what the framework is and is not: no minimum volume and no exclusivity. The purpose clause helps to read every other clause.

A framework agreement sets the rules for many future orders; it is not an order itself. Each order is a Call-Off. No minimum volume, no exclusivity, no guaranteed award: GER does not promise to order, and Meridian cannot count on work. The price of each Call-Off is charged to the Joint Account, so the JV partners (60/40) pay it. “Collaboration” does not make GER and Meridian partners.

2 Definitions · Call-Off, Change Order, Contract Price, Deliverables, Protected Liabilities, SOW
Clause 2 · DefinitionsDICTIONARYwhat the capitalised words mean

Why it matters. All capitalised terms get their meaning here; D3 defines them carefully but the wrong name for a party (Licensor) can still cause confusion.

Call-Off = a signed order. Change Order = a signed change to a Call-Off. Contract Price = the price in the Call-Off, adjusted by Change Orders. Protected Liabilities = fraud, wilful misconduct, gross negligence and anything the law does not allow parties to limit: these are never capped.

3 Governance and cooperation · each party names a contract representative and a project representative · a governance meeting does not amend the contract
Clause 3 · Governance and cooperationTEAMwho speaks for each side

Why it matters. It says who speaks and decides for each side, so a decision can be traced to a person.

Each side names a contract representative (contract changes, notices) and a project representative (daily coordination). A governance meeting does not itself amend the contract: what is said in meetings does not change what was signed.

4 Call-Off formation · a Call-Off becomes effective only when both parties sign it · an email or a purchase order is not a Call-Off · no chargeable work before that
Clause 4 · Call-Off formationORDER FORMhow a Call-Off becomes real

Why it matters. A Call-Off is the actual order: until it is signed by both sides, no chargeable work and no payment (a condition precedent).

A Call-Off is the order form: scope, deliverables, price, milestones, acceptance criteria. It becomes effective only when both sign. A quotation, purchase order or routine email does not create one, and Meridian must not begin chargeable work before. This is a condition precedent: the signed Call-Off comes first. Practical risk: work that starts on an email.

5 Order of precedence · signed amendment, then this Agreement, then the Call-Off, then the SOW · a lower document may override only if it names the clause and is signed by someone with authority · Schedule 1 says "Approved departures: None"
Clause 5 · Order of precedenceRANKINGwhich document wins when they disagree

Why it matters. It settles conflicts between documents: a ranking list is the cheapest insurance against contradictions.

If documents conflict, the order is: signed amendment, this Agreement, the signed Call-Off, its SOW, technical schedules. A lower document may override the Agreement only if it names the clause, says it intends to override and is signed by someone with authority.

Why ambiguous? Schedule 1 says “Approved departures: None”, but Schedule 1 itself contains two departures: a time bar for late notice and deemed acceptance of Mechanical Completion. The Call-Off contradicts its own statement.

6 Performance standard · professional care, qualified people, agreed specifications
Clause 6 · Performance standardQUALITYthe standard of work

Why it matters. It sets the level of work against which breaches are measured.

“Professional care and competence” is the level of a careful expert, not a guarantee of perfection. It is a judgement standard, so a Call-Off should add measurable specifications.

7 GER inputs and site access · GER provides the inputs allocated to it · the Contractor checks them for obvious inconsistencies
Clause 7 · GER inputs and site accessGER’S PARTwhat GER must provide

Why it matters. It lists what GER must provide so the contractor cannot say that it was delayed by GER’s failure unless it really was.

GER must supply the inputs allocated to it (data, access). The Contractor must check them for obvious inconsistencies and tell GER. If it does not, that does not automatically make the Contractor responsible for GER’s data: responsibility follows the express allocation.

8 Programme and time relief · the Contractor must notify an event within 10 Business Days · GER assesses within 15 Business Days · late notice matters "only if the delay prejudices" here, but is "barred" in Schedule 1
Clause 8 · Programme and time reliefCLOCKtime, delays and late notice

Why it matters. It controls time: when a delay is excused and by when it must be reported. Late notice can lose the relief.

Time relief = extra time, without penalty, when a delay is not the Contractor’s fault. The Contractor must notify within 10 Business Days of becoming aware of the event.

The conflict. Clause 8 says a late notice affects relief only if the delay prejudices GER’s assessment or mitigation; Schedule 1 says a late claim “is barred”, with no such test. Which wins? Clause 5 says the Agreement prevails over the Call-Off unless a departure was approved, and Schedule 1 says there are none.

9 Changes · a change request states its effect on scope, price and programme · nothing binds before signature
Clause 9 · ChangesCHANGEhow the work can be changed

Why it matters. It prevents informal changes that nobody has priced: every change has a request, an effect on price and time, and a signature.

A change request must state its effect on scope, price, programme, testing and risk. Nobody has to implement a commercial change before it is signed. In an immediate safety emergency, the Contractor acts first and the parties settle the money afterwards.

10 Delivery and acceptance · a rejection must state the criteria · deemed acceptance only if the Call-Off says so, and Schedule 1 does, for Mechanical Completion
Clause 10 · Delivery and acceptanceHAND-OVERdelivery and acceptance

Why it matters. It decides when work is accepted: acceptance starts payment and warranty periods.

Acceptance is GER’s agreement that the work meets the criteria. Receiving the goods is not acceptance. Deemed acceptance means silence counts as acceptance: if GER does not answer within 15 Business Days, the work is accepted. Clause 10 allows it only if the Call-Off says so with its trigger; Schedule 1 does so for Mechanical Completion (a risk for GER).

11 Prices, invoices and payment · prices come from the Call-Off · GER pays undisputed amounts within 60 days
Clause 11 · Prices, invoices and paymentPAYMENTinvoices and the 60 days

Why it matters. It is the money clause: valid invoice, 60 days, disputed amounts. The clock for interest and suspension starts here.

Prices come from the Call-Off. GER pays undisputed amounts within 60 days of a valid invoice. What GER disputes it must identify, with reasons, and it must keep paying the rest. No set-off (deducting what it says Meridian owes) of disputed amounts unless the law or the contract allows it.

12 Warranties and defects · 24 months · repair, replace or reperform
Clause 12 · Warranties and defectsGUARANTEEwarranty and defects

Why it matters. It sets how long defects are covered and what the contractor must do (repair, replace, re-perform).

The Contractor guarantees that the deliverables meet the specifications. The warranty lasts 24 months from the event in the Call-Off (Final Acceptance in Call-Off No. 1). For a defect it must repair, replace or reperform; if it does not, GER can have it fixed elsewhere and recover the documented cost, within the caps.

13 Sustainability and environmental obligations · each biofuel Call-Off identifies feedstock, criteria, data and evidence
Clause 13 · Sustainability and environmental obligationsGREENsustainability data for biofuel

Why it matters. It makes the contractor responsible for the data GER needs for biofuel sustainability reports; mistakes here have regulatory consequences.

For biofuel, each Call-Off must say what it is made from, which sustainability criteria apply, how carbon intensity is measured and who supplies each set of data. Whoever supplies data must make it accurate and traceable.

14 Environmental indemnity · the Contractor reimburses clean-up costs and third-party claims it causes · mixed causes are shared
Clause 14 · Environmental indemnityCLEAN-UPwho pays for pollution

Why it matters. It says who pays for pollution and how losses are shared if both contributed. It sits under its own cap.

The environmental indemnity: if the Contractor’s contaminated materials or its breach of handling rules cause pollution, it reimburses GER’s investigation and clean-up costs and third-party claims, but only for the part it caused. Mixed causes are shared. These amounts have their own cap (EUR 20,000,000, clause 16.2).

15 Delay damages · the sole monetary remedy for delay · reaching the cap does not end the Call-Off · Schedule 1: "No termination cut-off specified"
Clause 15 · Delay damagesLATE FEEdelay damages

Why it matters. It fixes the price of delay in advance. Because it is the sole monetary remedy, GER cannot claim more for the same delay.

Delay damages are a daily amount agreed in advance as compensation for delay. In Call-Off No. 1, for example, Final Acceptance costs EUR 30,000 a day up to EUR 2,520,000, with a total cap of EUR 4,200,000. They are the sole monetary remedy for the delay.

The weakness. Schedule 1 says “No termination cut-off specified”, and reaching the cap does not end the Call-Off. After EUR 4,200,000 the Contractor could keep being late at no further cost. GER could still end the Call-Off for convenience on 60 days’ notice (clause 20), but it would pay for the work done.

16 Liability allocation · cap of 100% of the Call-Off price, minimum EUR 10,000,000; environmental cap EUR 20,000,000; no lost profit; fraud and gross negligence never capped
Clause 16 · Liability allocationLIMITcaps and excluded losses

Why it matters. It tells everyone the most they can lose, what is never recoverable and what has no cap at all.

The general cap is 100% of the Call-Off price with a minimum of EUR 10,000,000: for Call-Off No. 1 (EUR 42,000,000) that is EUR 42,000,000. A separate EUR 20,000,000 cap covers environmental claims and does not use up the general cap. Loss of profit, revenue and production are excluded, except the amounts 16.4 lists (delay damages, defect correction, environmental indemnity, confidentiality incident costs). Protected Liabilities have no cap. Compare: D2 caps at USD 25,000,000 and Annex I at 12 months of royalties: three ceilings in one project.

17 Intellectual property and confidentiality · each keeps its own IP · secrets stay under "the NDA dated 7 September 2026" (not D1)
Clause 17 · Intellectual property and confidentialitySECRETSown IP and confidentiality

Why it matters. It says who owns what and how information is kept secret during and after the contract.

Each party keeps its own pre-existing IP. For confidentiality D3 points to “the NDA dated 7 September 2026”. That NDA is not D1 and is not in our pack: treat it as a document referred to but not seen.

18 Insurance and records · insurance listed in Schedule 3 · records kept for 10 years · GER may audit
Clause 18 · Insurance and recordsSAFETY NETinsurance and records

Why it matters. It makes the contractor carry insurance and records, so a claim can actually be paid and proved.

The Contractor must hold the insurance listed in Schedule 3. Insurance does not enlarge the caps. Both parties keep records for 10 years after Final Acceptance and GER may audit them.

19 Suspension · GER may suspend by notice · the Contractor may suspend after 15 days for a serious safety risk or overdue payment
Clause 19 · SuspensionPAUSEsuspension

Why it matters. It lets GER pause the work (and the contractor stop for non-payment or safety). The notice and cure steps are the key.

GER may pause the work by notice. The Contractor may pause only for a serious safety risk or a material overdue undisputed payment, after a notice and cure period of 15 days. Note: 15 days here, 30 days to terminate, 10 days in Annex I F.2 and 30 days in D2 11.1(a): four clocks in one project.

20 Termination · material breach not cured within 30 days; GER may end a Call-Off for convenience on 60 days’ notice
Clause 20 · TerminationEXITtermination

Why it matters. It is the exit clause: for cause after 30 days’ cure, or for convenience on 60 days’ notice.

Two ways out of a Call-Off: (1) a material breach not fixed within 30 days of notice (or sooner if it cannot be fixed); (2) convenience termination: GER may end a Call-Off for no reason on 60 days’ notice, paying for work done, approved commitments and demobilisation, less avoided costs, with no profit on unperformed work. Ending the framework does not end existing Call-Offs.

21 Events beyond reasonable control · notify promptly · either party may end the affected Call-Off after 90 days
Clause 21 · Events beyond reasonable controlEXCUSEevents beyond reasonable control

Why it matters. It excuses events beyond control but protects payments for completed work. It is the D3 version of D2 Article 6.

Same idea as D2 Article 6. Better than D2: payment for completed work is not excused, and either party may end the affected Call-Off after 90 days. Still vague: “promptly”.

22 General and dispute provisions · Italian law; courts of Milan after 20 Business Days of escalation · notices take effect on "confirmed receipt"
Clause 22 · General and dispute provisionsREFEREE AND POSTBOXlaw, courts, notices

Why it matters. Law, courts, escalation and notices: where disputes go and how formal messages are sent.

Italian law and the courts of Milan, after 20 Business Days of escalation to senior representatives. D2 uses English law and ICC London: two laws and two forums in one project.

Notices take effect on confirmed receipt (the receiver must confirm), while D2 14.2 presumes receipt by dates. If the receiver stays silent, was the notice received?

SCHEDULES · 1 Call-Off Form (Call-Off No. 1, EUR 42,000,000) · 2 Authority register · 3 Insurance · 4 Notices
SchedulesFORMS AND LISTSthe filled-in forms

Why it matters. The filled-in forms (Call-Off No. 1, price, scope) are what the parties actually ordered.

Schedule 1 is the Call-Off Form, filled in for Call-Off No. 1 (EUR 42,000,000; milestones to 31 October 2028). Schedule 2 says who may sign what (Marchetti: Change Orders and NDAs up to EUR 5,000,000; nothing for larger Change Orders). Schedule 3 is insurance; Schedule 4, notice addresses.

Colour code for the X-ray

Yellow the most important information · Purple what looks ambiguous or unclear to you

💡 SUGGESTED DRAFTING · when you have organised your ideas, click here (or press Check) to open the clause in plain English.
SUGGESTED DRAFTING · plain English, same purpose. Use it as feedback on how you organised the clause.

ID card · D3 (framework). Parties: GER (acting as Operator of the JV) and Meridian Offshore Systems Ltd; 18 January 2027. Purpose: a framework for the supply, logistics and integration work of Project Horizon; no minimum volume, no exclusivity (clause 1). Key duty: each order is a Call-Off that becomes effective only when both sign (clause 4); the Contractor performs with agreed professional care (clause 6). Money: price stated in each Call-Off and charged to the Joint Account (clauses 1, 11); delay damages are the sole monetary remedy for delay (clause 15). Risk: general cap of 100% of the Call-Off price, minimum EUR 10,000,000 (16.1); separate environmental cap of EUR 20,000,000 (16.2); Protected Liabilities never capped (16.5). Exit: 30 days to cure a material breach; GER may terminate a Call-Off for convenience on 60 days’ notice (clause 20). Law: Italian law; Milan courts after 20 Business Days of escalation (clause 22).

Three of the nine elements to look for: schedules (Call-Off Form), order of precedence (clause 5) and signatures.

CLAUSE PROFILE · The three ID cards (D2, Annex I, D3)

What it is and its job. Three contracts that fit together: D2 is the partnership, Annex I is a licence inside it, D3 is the framework GER signs for the venture.

What it should contain. Each ID card should have the same seven headings: parties, purpose, key duty, money, risk, exit, law. If two participants write different headings, the cards cannot be compared.

Why it matters in Project Horizon. Participants will spend the whole week with these three documents. An ID card is the habit of reading any contract in seven lines before reading it in full.

How it relates to the other contracts. D2 and Annex I are one contract. D3 is signed by GER as Operator: the venture pays, so PETROX bears 40% of what D3 costs. D3 gives its own law (Italian) while D2 uses English law: two laws in one project.

SHAPING THE EXERCISE · what to ask while they organize

Ask: Which of the seven headings was hardest to fill? (usually "key duty").

Ask: Where do two ID cards disagree? (law: English in D2, Italian in D3).

Do not read the cards for them: let two or three participants read theirs first.

Point at a heading in the X-ray and ask: what do you think this article does? Give the one-word label (it sits under each line of your X-ray) only after they try.

TRANSITION

Now we check the ID cards against the nine elements: where in each contract do the recitals, the definitions, the warranties and the boilerplate live?

Element by element · what each part is for

Open each card when we reach that part. Every card says: which part of the contract it belongs to, where you find it in the Horizon documents, what it is for, and what it looks like.

1 Recitals · the background

Part: Preliminary · Where in Horizon: NDA (WHEREAS paragraphs); D3 clause 1 (purpose)

Purpose. To tell the story: who the parties are and why they sign. No rule belongs here.

Before the recitals: the title (“This ___ AGREEMENT”), the date (“the Effective Date”) and the parties: identify each person or legal entity by full registered name and type (domestic or foreign company). If you have the registration and tax details of the companies, write them down (in other systems: company, permanent account and tax identification numbers).

Heading: RECITALS or BACKGROUND. WHEREAS, no operative clauses should go in this section; WHEREAS, only the general information.

Lead-in: The parties agree as follows:

Avoid the old bridge “NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the covenants and agreements hereinafter set forth, and for other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which is hereby acknowledged, the parties hereto agree as follows”. The plain lead-in does the same job.

2 Definitions

Part: Preliminary · Where in Horizon: D2 Article 1; D3 clause 2; NDA 1.1

Purpose. To give each important word one meaning for the whole contract.

Looks like: “As used in this Agreement, the following words and phrases have the meanings set out below unless a different meaning is plainly required by the context:” followed by an alphabetical list.

Define a term once, use it with the same capital letters everywhere, and do not let two definitions refer to each other (see Pair 4 in Ex 5.9).

3 Agreements · the obligations (example: an NDA)

Part: Operative · Where in Horizon: NDA clause 2; Annex I Section C

Purpose. To say who must do what. This is the heart of the agreement: the rights and obligations of the parties.

An NDA must contain: (1) the commitment not to use the Confidential Information for a purpose other than the one agreed; (2) the obligation to receive and hold it in strict confidence; (3) reasonable efforts / best efforts to prevent disclosure (reasonable care means at least the level of care you would use to protect your own confidential information); (4) the obligation not to disclose to a third party without the written approval of the disclosing party (restrictions on use and no disclosure); (5) the acknowledgement that the Confidential Information is, and will remain, the exclusive property of the disclosing party.

4 Conditions precedent

Part: Operative · Where in Horizon: D3 clause 4 (no chargeable work without a signed Call-Off)

Purpose. To say what must happen first, before the contract or a part of it comes into effect.

A condition precedent (CP) is a requirement or event that must happen before the contract, or certain parts of it, can come into effect.

What does it look like? “It shall be a condition precedent…” · “If… then…” · “Until…” · “Provided that…”.

5 Representations and warranties

Part: Operative · Where in Horizon: D2 Article 9; NDA 6.1–6.2; Annex I E (as-is)

Purpose. To state facts that are true today, so that the other party can rely on them. If the facts are false, there are consequences.

To make a representation means to make a statement of fact that is truthful and accurate. In many non-common-law systems “representation” and “warranty” are the same concept and are interchangeable; under English law they relate to different things: a representation is a statement of fact made to induce the other party to enter into the contract; a warranty is a promise in the contract.

Example: “Each Party affirms that it owns and has rights to its Intellectual Property for conducting business.” What could be the purpose of inserting this clause? (so that each party can rely on the other’s ownership; if it is false, there is a claim).

NDA 6.1 · Preceding Disclosures. The Receiving Party confirms that Confidential Information already disclosed in relation to the Purpose, and any discussions already held between them from 15 March 2020 and thereafter, shall be subject to the Agreement.
6.2 · Warranty. The Receiving Party warrants that, between the date in 6.1 and the date of the Agreement, it has not disclosed, done or omitted anything that would have been a breach if the Agreement had been in force. Purpose: to cover the period before signature.

Pre-contractual statements: if they are incorrect, what is the consequence? See the chart in Case 2.

6 Boilerplate · standard clauses

Part: Boilerplate · Where in Horizon: D2 Articles 12–15; D3 clauses 20–22; NDA 8

Purpose. Standard end clauses that look alike in every contract. They are adapted to the needs of the situation after negotiation.

Table of the standard clauses (in the next table) with an example and where to find it in Horizon.

ClauseWhat it doesExampleIn Horizon
AssignmentStops a party from handing the contract to someone else“This Agreement will not be assigned, in whole or in part, by any party without the written consent of the other party.”D2 Art. 12
AmendmentSays how the contract may be changed“This Agreement cannot be modified in any way except in writing signed by all the parties.”D2 15.2
ConfidentialityKeeps information secret(the NDA itself is the model)NDA 2; Annex I C
CounterpartsAllows signing in separate copies“This Agreement may be executed in counterparts.” (the handout lists this sentence under “confidentiality”: it is a counterparts clause)D2 15.5
Dispute resolutionSays how disputes are handled“If a dispute arises, the Parties will try to resolve it through negotiation or mediation before starting a court action.”D2 Art. 13; D3 22
Force majeureExcuses events beyond control. Ask: in case of what, when, how, what then?“No party is liable for delay caused by acts beyond its control, to the extent of the delay.”D2 Art. 6; D3 21
Governing law / jurisdictionChooses the law and the place of the dispute“This agreement is governed by the laws of Italy.”D2 13.1; D3 22
HeadingsHeadings are for convenience, not for interpretation“Headings are inserted for the convenience of the parties only and are not considered when interpreting this Agreement.”(check)
IndemnificationA promise to pay“Each Party agrees to indemnify the other against liabilities arising from negligence.”D2 Art. 5
Entire agreement (integration / merger)The written contract is the whole deal“The Agreement is the entire agreement and understanding between the parties and supersedes all prior communications, contracts or agreements on its subject, oral or written.”(check)
Limitation of damagesSets a limit for each party’s liability“Neither Party will be liable for indirect or consequential damages. Liability Cap. A Party’s liability is limited to the Fees paid.”D2 Art. 10; D3 16
NoticeSays how formal messages must be sentState how notices must be given (written, hand-delivered, registered post), for electronic notices whether a confirmation of delivery is needed, and whether business days count (then define them).D2 Art. 14; NDA 8.4
Severability (saving clause)If one part is void, the rest survives“If any part of this Agreement is declared unenforceable or invalid, the remainder will continue to be valid and enforceable.”D2 15.5
TerminationSays when a party may end the contractTermination of the Agreement also ends active service agreements. For cause: the Service Provider may terminate if the Customer breaches or fails to pay. For convenience: a party may terminate for any reason, with notice.D2 Art. 11; D3 20

No waiverNot enforcing a right now does not lose it“The failure or delay of a party to enforce any right or remedy is not a waiver of it, and does not prevent its later exercise.” (the handout lists this under “warranty clause”)D2 15.5
7 Schedules, signatures, appendices

Part: Boilerplate · Where in Horizon: D2 Schedules 1–3; Annex I Exhibit A-1; D3 Schedule 1 and signature blocks

Purpose. To keep the detail (price lists, maps, forms, names) out of the main text, and to show who signed, in what role and when.

Schedules are the detailed information (for example price lists); a schedule is part of the contract if the contract says so.

TEACHER NOTE · how to run Ex 5.4

What this exercise trains. Reading a contract by function: before reading the words, ask "what is this part for?" The nine elements are the nine possible answers.

In one line each (say it in simple words). (a) Definitions: "X means…", the dictionary of the contract. (b) Representations and warranties: "each Party represents that…", a statement that something is true today. (c) Agreements (operative clauses): "shall issue… shall pay…", who must do what. (d) Boilerplate: standard end-of-contract rules that look alike in every contract (for example "no waiver"). (e) and (g) Schedules: tables, forms and lists attached at the back; (e) is a table of names, (g) is a form to fill in. (h) Signatures: who signs, in what role, on what date.

(f) is the hard one. A condition precedent is something that must happen first, before something else can start. Simple example: you cannot drive the car until you have the key. In D3 the “key” is a signed Call-Off: without it, Meridian cannot start chargeable work and GER does not have to pay. Expected answer: 3. If a participant says 4 (agreements), ask: “What has to happen first?” They will answer “the signed Call-Off”, and that is the condition. The sentence is written as a prohibition (“must not begin”), which is why some people read it as a plain duty; both readings are understandable, but the useful idea is “this comes first”.

What are recitals? The opening paragraphs, usually starting WHEREAS, that explain why the parties are signing (for example “GER owns seismic data; PETROX wishes to evaluate it”). They tell the story; they are not the rules. The NDA (D1) has WHEREAS paragraphs; D2, Annex I and D3 do not: they go straight to the parties, a purpose clause or definitions. Plain-English drafters call “WHEREAS” archaic. Ask: is the missing recital a gap or a choice? A purpose clause (D3 clause 1) does the same job in ordinary words, and it is written as part of the rules (verify how a court treats each).

WHEREAS is archaic and not necessary. It is a relic of old English contracts: one very long sentence broken into “whereas” pieces. Nothing in the law requires the word. Recitals themselves are optional; the contract works without them. If you want the background, you can say it in plain words. How to replace it: (1) Use a heading, Background (or Purpose), and short numbered sentences: “A. GER owns seismic data for Blocks 14/06 and 15/07. B. PETROX wishes to evaluate that data to decide whether to enter into a joint venture with GER.” (2) Close with a bridge in ordinary words: “The parties agree as follows:” instead of “NOW, THEREFORE, the parties hereto agree as follows”. (3) Or put a purpose clause at clause 1, as D3 does: “This Agreement sets out the terms on which…”. Warning for the NDA: its second recital also defines “the Permitted Purpose”, so the recital is doing the work of a definition. Whatever you do, a defined term must live in the definitions or in the rules, not hidden in the story.

POSSIBLE QUESTIONS · ANSWERS

Q: Is a schedule part of the contract? A: Yes, if the contract says so. D2 Art. 1 says the Agreement includes its Schedules, Exhibits and Annexes.

Q: What is the difference between a schedule and an appendix? A: Schedules are binding parts: lists, tables, procedures. Appendices only support the text. Check the contract: if it says "forms part of", it binds.

Case 2The hops and the sulphur10 minJV · D2

A case about one sentence: was it a representation or a term of the contract? Read, follow the guide, predict, then reveal how the court decided.

Part of the contractOperative section · representations and warranties
Clause / headingD2 Article 9 and NDA 6.2 (statements of fact); Annex I Section E (as-is)
Why it mattersIf a statement is false, the consequence depends on its type: no consequence, a claim for misrepresentation, or a breach of contract.
Pre-contractual statement
Mere puffIf false → no consequences
RepresentationIf false → liability (misrepresentation) → damages only if fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation → loss suffered
TermIf false → liability (breach of contract) → automatic right to damages → generally the expectation interest
Issue

Whether the defendant’s assurance regarding whether the hops had received a sulphur treatment constituted a representation or a contractually enforceable term.

Facts

The claimant, Bannerman, formed a contract with the defendant, White, regarding the purchase of hops, intending to use them to produce beer. The claimant specifically enquired as to whether the hops had received a sulfur treatment as it is only possible to make usable beer from hops that have not received this treatment. Furthermore, the claimant expressly stated that he would be unwilling to buy the hops if they had been treated. The defendant assured the claimant that the hops were untreated, however in fact the hops had received sulfur treatment and were subsequently useless to the claimant; thus Bannerman brought an action against White for damages, contending that the statement regarding treatment ought to be viewed as a contractual term which White had thus breached.

Follow the reading · before the answer
  1. Read the facts and underline the claimant’s question and his statement that he would not buy treated hops.
  2. Ask: would the buyer have bought the hops without the assurance? How important was it to him, and did the seller know?
  3. Choose a box in the chart: mere puff, representation or term? Think about what each box would give the buyer if the statement is false.
  4. Write your prediction: who wins, and which box is it?
How the court decided. The court held that the assurance was a term of the contract (a condition), not just a representation: the buyer had made it clear that the question was essential and that he would not buy otherwise, and the seller knew it. So the seller was in breach of contract and the buyer could claim damages. Lesson: a statement that is important to the deal should be written into the contract as a term or warranty, so nobody has to argue about its status later. Horizon link: D2 Article 9 and NDA 6.2 do exactly that; Annex I E (“as is”) does the opposite, by saying what GER does not promise.
In Horizon, GER tells PETROX in a meeting: “SeismoCore will run on any of your servers.” The sentence does not appear in Annex I. In which box is it most likely to fall?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ A term must be part of the contract: Bannerman v White was decided on the buyer’s insistence.
✗ It matters: false pre-contract statements can lead to claims.
✓ A statement that stays outside the contract is much harder to enforce. If it matters, write it in (Annex I Schedule A-2 lists the approved infrastructure) and, if you do not want to promise it, say so (E.2, “as is”). Many contracts also add an entire-agreement clause.
TEACHER NOTE · Case 2

Instructor note. Distinguish three questions: (1) was the statement a term or a representation (this case)? (2) is it true? (3) what is the remedy? Under English law the test looks at the importance of the statement to the parties and whether it was meant to be relied on (verify the details with counsel). Italian law has different tools (pre-contractual good faith, Art. 1337 Civil Code, and error or deceit): do not map one system onto the other. The chart is from the handout; the sentence “GER will run on any servers” is invented for the course.
