C. Commercial terms and their language

TRANSITION

"Money and time are where the language costs the most. A wrong comma in a royalty clause is a million euros. Three exercises: a royalty clause with problems, the money-and-time words, and the caps in D3."

Ex 5.6Clause Lab · the royalty (D2 Article 3.1)15 minJV · D2

On your own. First read the two money words. Then highlight the clause: yellow for the price, pink for what changes the price. Then compare with the plain version and answer the four questions.

Part of the contractOperative · the price
Clause / headingD2 Article 3.1 · Royalty
Why it mattersEvery unclear word in a price clause is money in dispute.
TEACHER SAYS · before Ex 5.6 · ★ core · individual work

“Work on your own, not in pairs. Step 1, 3 minutes: read the box ‘In simple words’. Step 2, 4 minutes: highlight clause 3.1. Yellow is the price: who pays whom, how much, on what. Pink is what changes the price: the deductions, the limit, the multiplier and who may change it. Press Check and compare with the organised version. Step 3, 8 minutes: read the plain-English version and answer the four questions.”

In simple words · what clause 3.1 says

The idea. PETROX uses GER’s software. In return PETROX pays GER a royalty: a percentage of the money PETROX earns from the oil and gas produced with that software. Think of a rent that grows when PETROX earns more.

Gross Revenue = the whole amount. All the money PETROX receives from selling the oil and gas, before taking anything off.

Net Revenue = what is left after the allowed deductions. Gross Revenue minus the costs the contract lets PETROX subtract (the definition is in Schedule 3, Part A). The royalty is calculated on this smaller number: 3.5% of Net Revenue.

The deduction limit. PETROX cannot subtract as much as it likes. The limit in 3.1 is 20% of the Gross Revenue in a quarter. Example (invented numbers): Gross Revenue USD 20,000,000, so the limit is USD 4,000,000. If PETROX spent USD 5,000,000 on third parties, it can subtract only USD 4,000,000, and Net Revenue is USD 16,000,000.

The multiplier. A number from a table that moves the royalty up or down. 3.1 says the table is in “Schedule 3, Part B, Column 4”.

Who must do what. PETROX must pay the royalty (a duty). GER may change the multiplier table on 60 days’ written notice (a right). Under 3.2 GER may audit PETROX’s books once a year, with 5 Business Days’ notice (a right).

Left: the original. Highlight and press Send to collect your marks in Organize (under the original). Right: the same deal in plain English. Highlight it the same way (yellow = the price, pink = what changes the price) and compare how short the pink part has become.

Original · D2 Article 3.1

① Pick a tool. ② Click words, or drag across them. Click again with the same tool to undo. Everyone works differently: there is no single right way to mark.

3.1 In consideration of the licence granted hereunder, the Licensee shall pay to the Licensor a royalty calculated as follows: Base Royalty Rate: Three and one-half percent (3.5%) of Net Revenue attributable to production from wells in which the Licensed Technology was utilised in any phase of exploration, appraisal, or development operations, less and except any amounts attributable to third-party costs incurred by the Licensee in connection with the deployment of the Licensed Technology, provided that such deductions shall not in any event exceed twenty percent (20%) of the Gross Revenue generated from the relevant wells in any given Calendar Quarter, adjusted upwards or downwards in accordance with the Production Volume Multiplier Table set forth in Schedule 3, Part B, Column 4, as may from time to time be amended by GER upon sixty (60) days’ written notice to PETROX.

💡 SUGGESTED DRAFTING · when you have organised your ideas, click here (or press Check) to open the clause in plain English.
SUGGESTED DRAFTING · plain English, same purpose. Use it as feedback on how you organised the clause.

Organised. Who pays whom: PETROX pays GER. How much: 3.5% of Net Revenue, from wells where the software was used. What can be subtracted: third-party costs of deploying the software. The limit: deductions at most 20% of Gross Revenue in a quarter. The multiplier: a number from a table in Schedule 3, Part B, Column 4. Who can change it: GER, on 60 days’ written notice.

Yellow is the price. Pink is what moves the price. A clear clause keeps them in different sentences: the original puts everything in one.

Plain English · same deal, clear structure
3.1 PETROX must pay GER a royalty on the Net Revenue from wells in which it used the Licensed Technology.
3.2 Definitions. “Gross Revenue” means all revenue PETROX receives in a Calendar Quarter from the sale of Petroleum produced from those wells, before deductions. “Permitted Deductions” means verified third-party costs that PETROX directly incurred to deploy the Licensed Technology; they must not exceed 20% of Gross Revenue in a Calendar Quarter. “Net Revenue” means Gross Revenue minus Permitted Deductions.
3.3 Formula. For each Calendar Quarter: royalty = Net Revenue × 3.5% × Volume Multiplier. The Volume Multiplier values are in one table only: [Schedule 3].
3.4 Changes. The Volume Multiplier values may be changed only by a written amendment signed by both Parties (Article 15.2).
3.5 Example (invented numbers). Gross Revenue USD 20,000,000. Third-party costs USD 5,000,000, but the limit is 20% × 20,000,000 = USD 4,000,000. Net Revenue = 16,000,000. With a multiplier of 1.15, royalty = 16,000,000 × 3.5% × 1.15 = USD 644,000.

INSTRUCTOR NOTE · read straight after the clauses, before the questions

The one-sentence idea. PETROX pays GER a share of its takings for using the software. Everything else in 3.1 only tells you how to count the takings.

Use a market stall. Say: “You sell fruit and receive EUR 20,000 in the month. That is your gross takings. The owner of the stall wants 3.5%, but not on the full EUR 20,000: first you may subtract some costs. What is left is your net takings. The rule says you may subtract costs, but never more than 20% of the gross, that is EUR 4,000. Even if your costs were EUR 5,000, you subtract only EUR 4,000. Net is EUR 16,000. The owner’s share is 3.5% of 16,000, that is EUR 560.” This is the royalty arithmetic without the multiplier.

Three questions right after they read. (1) Which colour is longer, yellow or pink? Pink: the price is short, the adjustments are long. (2) What does the deduction limit relate to? To the gross figure, not to the net one. (3) Who can change the multiplier, and how? GER, with 60 days’ notice.

“Shall” does not stand for duty. In plain-English drafting we do not use SHALL to mean “must”, because it has too many meanings: duty, future, permission, even a definition (“shall mean”). We use MUST for a duty, MAY for a right and WILL for a future step that needs no choice. Look at the original: “the Licensee shall pay” is a duty, but elsewhere the same word introduces a right (“shall have the right”) and a definition (“shall mean”). One word, three jobs. In the plain version: PETROX must pay (duty), GER may audit (right), the multiplier table will appear in Schedule 3 (future). Ask: who is the actor of each verb?

Watch for: what is the problem of not defining Gross Revenue and Net Revenue? D2 never defines Gross Revenue, and Net Revenue only in Schedule 3, Part A. (1) Without a definition each side reads “revenue” its own way: does it include sales to affiliates, gains on hedging, insurance payments, money invoiced but not yet received? Different readings give different royalties. (2) The 20% limit is calculated on Gross Revenue: if the base is unclear, the limit is unclear too. (3) Schedule 3 lists more deductions than 3.1 and says they have no percentage limit: the same word “Net Revenue” has two recipes. (4) At an audit under 3.2 the auditor needs a rule to apply; if none exists, the dispute goes to arbitration. The plain version defines both terms once, next to the formula, and adds a worked example.

In the original, the 3.5% applies to Net Revenue and the 20% limit to Gross Revenue. What does the plain version do about it?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ The limit is part of the deal: a language fix must not delete it.
✗ The rate is on Net Revenue: changing the base changes the price.
✓ Two bases in one sentence make the reader hunt. Definitions fix the names; the formula shows the order. The 20% limit is part of the deal, so it stays.
TEACHER NOTE · in simple words

Say: “Imagine your bonus is a percentage of your salary after tax, but the limit on the bonus is set on your salary before tax. Two numbers with similar names in the same sentence: you have to hunt for which one is meant. The plain version gives each number a name once.” Ask: which is bigger, gross or net? Gross. So 20% of gross is a bigger amount than 20% of net: 20% of 20,000,000 is 4,000,000, while 20% of 16,000,000 is 3,200,000. The base you choose changes how much can be deducted.

D2 Schedule 3, Part A says that Permitted Deductions “are not subject to any percentage limit”. Article 3.1 limits them to 20% of Gross Revenue. Which is true?
✗ Annex I B.2 points to Schedule 3, but 3.1 also deals with deductions.
✗ Position in the text does not decide.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✓ On audit, PETROX will quote the Schedule and GER the body. The plain version states the limit once in the definition. Order of precedence is a rule that must be written: here 15.3 covers only Annex I against D2.
TEACHER NOTE · in simple words

Say: “Two rooms of the same house give different rules for the same door. Clause 3.1 says deductions stop at 20%. Schedule 3 says there is no limit. Who wins? Nobody can tell.” Ask: who gains if there is no limit? PETROX, because it subtracts more and pays less royalty. Who gains if the limit is 20%? GER. So each side will quote the text that suits it: this is how a contradiction becomes a money dispute. Remind them that Schedule 3 also lists more kinds of deduction than 3.1 (transport, taxes, the Operator’s overhead).

In the original, GER may amend the multiplier table on 60 days’ notice. D2 15.2 says an amendment must be signed by both Parties. What follows?
✗ The multiplier changes the royalty directly.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ 3.1 is more specific and can be argued to prevail.
✓ A price that one party can change alone is commercially one-sided and unclear. The plain version allows a change only by signed amendment.
TEACHER NOTE · in simple words

Say: “Imagine a landlord who may change the rent by sending a letter, while the lease also says that any change must be signed by both. Which rule counts?” The plain version closes the question: only a signed amendment. Ask: is 60 days’ notice enough to be fair to PETROX? PETROX has no say in the change. What would you ask for if you were PETROX? (a signature, a maximum change per year, a right to end the licence if the change is too large).

Use the example in 3.5, but with no 20% limit (all USD 5,000,000 deducted). What would the royalty be at multiplier 1.15?
✗ That is with a multiplier of 1.00 and the limit.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ That is the result with the limit.
✓ (20,000,000 − 5,000,000) × 3.5% × 1.15 = 603,750. With the limit it is 644,000. The difference exists because the original leaves the limit doubtful: a worked example in the contract would settle it.
TEACHER NOTE · in simple words

Do it on the board. With the limit: 20,000,000 − 4,000,000 = 16,000,000; × 3.5% = 560,000; × 1.15 = 644,000. Without the limit: 20,000,000 − 5,000,000 = 15,000,000; × 3.5% = 525,000; × 1.15 = 603,750. The difference is 40,250 in one quarter, 161,000 in a year. Say: “A worked example inside the contract would stop this argument in one line.” A common mistake is to subtract 20% of the net figure: remind them that the limit relates to the gross.

CLAUSE PROFILE · D2 Article 3.1 (royalty)

What it is and its job. The money clause of the licence: what PETROX pays GER for using SeismoCore.

What it should contain. A rate; a base (Net or Gross Revenue); the deductions and their limit; a multiplier and where it is found; who may change it and with how much notice; the payment dates (3.2 audit and Annex I Section B).

Why it matters in Project Horizon. The royalty is the price PETROX pays GER for the software, so every unclear word is money in dispute. In simple terms: Gross Revenue is everything PETROX earns from the oil and gas; Net Revenue is what is left after the costs the contract allows; the 3.5% is calculated on that smaller figure. The deduction limit answers the question 'how much may PETROX subtract?' and the answer is 'up to 20% of the Gross figure'. So the clause works with two different bases in one sentence (Net for the rate, Gross for the limit), and Schedule 3 says there is no limit at all. In figures (invented): Gross 20,000,000, limit 4,000,000, Net at least 16,000,000, royalty with a 1.15 multiplier 644,000, and 603,750 if there were no limit.

How it relates to the other contracts. Annex I Section B sets tiers on "Annual Gross Revenue" and then says fees are calculated on "Net Revenue" (B.2). The two documents must use the same base. D2 15.3 and Annex I H.2 conflict on which prevails: until that is resolved, a royalty dispute has two answers.

SHAPING THE EXERCISE · what to ask while they organize

Ask: Which words give the formula? Which hide it?

Ask: Who may change the multiplier? With how much notice? (GER, 60 days). Is that fair to PETROX?

Ask: What is the base, Net or Gross? Where does each appear?

TRANSITION

Now the words that carry money and time across all the contracts.

Ex 5.7Money and time words8 minJV · D2

Seven phrases from three contracts. Say what each one does. Then solve the Gross or Net problem.

Part of the contractOperative · money and time
Clause / headingD2 8.3, 10.1, 10.2, 11.1(b) · Annex I F.2 · D3 15
Why it mattersWords that carry money and time are the ones that cost most when they are vague.
Reading rule · time of the essence

Time of the essence means that the timelines and schedules in the contract are strict: a late performance is a breach that can have its own consequences. Where the contract is silent, ask: what happens if we are one day late? In Horizon, check D3 clause 8 (time and delays) and D2 Article 7 (work programme).

TEACHER ONLY · small squares · say these first, in your own words
CASH CALLThe Operator asks the partners to send money in advance for the shared work. Each partner pays its share (D2 8.3). Like a group chat: “everyone put in EUR 100 for the rent”.
SECURED OVERNIGHT FINANCING RATE (SOFR)A benchmark US-dollar interest rate, published every business day, based on overnight loans backed by government bonds. “SOFR + 3” = the benchmark plus three percentage points. Gap in D2 8.3: which SOFR (overnight, average, term), on which date, and what if it is negative? A tight clause names the source, the date and says the rate is never below zero.
LIMITED“Limited to USD 25,000,000” is a ceiling: the most one party can ever pay. Always ask: per claim, per year or in total? D2 10.2 says “aggregate”, so in total, with exceptions (cash calls, royalties, Article 5).
INDIRECT OR CONSEQUENTIAL LOSSLoss that comes from the further effects of a breach, not from the breach itself (a lost contract, lost production). The words are technical and courts read them differently. D2 10.1 helps by also listing loss of production, profit or revenue. (Verify English and Italian rules.)
NOT REMEDIEDThe breach has not been put right. Open questions: does “remedied” mean stopped, repaired or paid for? Does the 30 days start when the notice is sent or when it is received?
RELEVANT MILESTONE DELAYD3 clause 15: delay damages apply only to a milestone that a Call-Off identifies, with its rate and cap. A delay in anything else is not covered.
REVENUEMoney coming in from sales, before costs. Not the same as profit.
GROSS REVENUEAll the money received from the sales, before taking anything off. D2 never defines it.
NET REVENUEGross Revenue minus the deductions the contract allows (Schedule 3, Part A). The royalty is calculated on it.
CURE PERIODThe time given to fix a breach before the other side can use the consequence (suspend, terminate). 30 days in D2 11.1(b), 10 days in Annex I F.2, 15 days in the D3 suspension rule.
UNDISPUTED AMOUNTThe part of a bill that nobody challenges. It must be paid on time even if another part is disputed.
SOLE MONETARY REMEDYThe only money compensation for that event. Other remedies, such as ending the contract, are not removed unless the clause says so.

TEACHER NOTE · one word for each part of a clause (only for you)

How to use. Whenever you review a clause (in the X-rays, here or later), ask “What does it do?” and let them answer in one word. These are the words, for you only. Say them after they try.

The seven phrases above. (a) DEADLINE · (b) INTEREST (the price of being late) · (c) CAP (the ceiling) · (d) EXCLUSION (losses nobody pays) · (e) CURE (time to fix it) · (f) TRIGGER (what starts the clock) · (g) ONLY REMEDY (the one compensation allowed).

The parts of one sentence. Take D2 8.3: “The Operator shall issue cash calls monthly. Each Party shall pay its Participating Interest share within twenty (20) days after receipt of the cash call. Late payments bear interest at three percentage points above SOFR.” WHO: the Operator, each Party · DUTY: shall issue, shall pay · WHAT: cash calls, a share · HOW OFTEN: monthly · HOW MUCH: the Participating Interest share · DEADLINE: within 20 days · CONSEQUENCE: interest at SOFR + 3. Ask them to find the same parts in another clause, for example D3 clause 11 (WHO: GER · DUTY: must pay · WHAT: undisputed amounts · DEADLINE: 60 days after a valid invoice).

The one-word labels for whole articles (the same ones you have under each X-ray in Ex 5.3): DICTIONARY, PERMISSION, PRICE, OWNERSHIP, OWN LOSS, EXCUSE, PLAN, MANAGER, TRUTH, LIMIT, EXIT, NO SWAPPING, REFEREE, POSTBOX, SMALL PRINT.

Quick game. Read a clause aloud without its heading and ask for the word. D2 10.2 “limited to USD 25,000,000” → LIMIT. D2 13.2 “ICC arbitration, seat London” → REFEREE. D2 14.1 “delivered by hand, by courier or by email” → POSTBOX. D3 20 “terminate… on 60 days’ notice” → EXIT.

Annex I B.1 sets the royalty tiers by Annual Gross Revenue. B.2 says all fees are calculated on Net Revenue. What is the problem?
✗ Schedule 3 defines Net Revenue as Gross Revenue less Permitted Deductions: different measures.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ Net Revenue is Gross minus deductions: it is smaller.
✓ Choose one measure and use it in the tiers and in the fee, or say clearly: "tier by Gross Revenue, fee on Net Revenue" and give an example. Without a worked example the clause is open to dispute.
A JV partner is 25 days late with a cash call and GER sends a written notice. Which two rules start to run?
✗ 10.2 is a cap, not a clock.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ D3 is with Meridian.
✓ Two different clocks: 10 days for the software, 30 days for default. Mismatched clocks are a drafting risk: flag them to the client.
Ex 5.8Caps: which claim falls where?5 minFRAMEWORK · D3

D3 clause 16 has four different treatments. Drag each claim to the right one.

Part of the contractOperative · limitation of liability
Clause / headingD3 clause 16 · Liability allocation
Why it mattersShows how much one party can lose or claim, and what no cap can touch.
TEACHER SAYS · before Ex 5.8 · individual work

"Work on your own. Clause 16 of D3 has four rooms. Read the left box: it explains each room in simple words. Then look at the right box: there are six claims. Put each claim in the room where it belongs. Method: ask the questions in order. Is it lost profit? Then room C. Is it fraud or gross negligence? Then room D. Is it a clean-up claim under clause 14? Then room B. Anything else, room A."

"Do not read the clause line by line: first understand the four rooms, then relate each claim to its room."

Limitation and exemption clauses · what they are for

Limitation of damages sets a limit for each party’s liability under the contract. Exemption clauses try to limit or exclude liability, and the exemption clause must be part of the contract to work.

Examples: “Neither Party will be liable for indirect or consequential damages.” · “Liability Cap. A Party’s liability is limited to the Fees paid.”

TEACHER ONLY · small squares · terms in clause 16
CAPThe ceiling on what a party can be made to pay in total. Above the cap nothing more is owed.
CALL-OFF PRICEThe price agreed in each Call-Off (clause 16.1 calls it the Contract Price of that Call-Off). The general cap is 100% of it, but never less than EUR 10,000,000.
ENVIRONMENTAL CAPA second, separate ceiling of EUR 20,000,000 for clean-up claims under clause 14. It does not use up the general cap: two buckets, not one.
ENVIRONMENTAL INDEMNITY AMOUNTSMoney the Contractor must reimburse to GER for investigation, containment and clean-up costs and third-party claims caused by it (clause 14). 16.4 keeps them recoverable, within the environmental cap.
EXCLUDED LOSSLoss that nobody can claim at all: lost profit, revenue, production, use or business opportunity, direct or indirect (16.3). Exception in 16.4: delay damages, defect correction, environmental amounts and confidentiality incident costs remain recoverable.
PROTECTED LIABILITIESFraud, wilful misconduct, gross negligence and anything the law does not let the parties limit. No cap and no exclusion applies (16.5).
CLAUSE 16 IN FOUR ROOMS · simple words

A · General cap (16.1). Ordinary claims, for example a defect. The most a party can ever owe is 100% of the Call-Off price, and at least EUR 10,000,000.

B · Environmental cap (16.2). Clean-up claims under clause 14. Their own ceiling: EUR 20,000,000. It is separate from A.

C · Excluded loss (16.3). Lost profit, revenue, production, use or business opportunity: nobody can claim them. Careful: 16.4 keeps delay damages, defect correction, clean-up amounts and confidentiality incident costs recoverable (each within its cap).

D · No cap (16.5). Fraud, wilful misconduct, gross negligence and what the law does not allow to limit. No cap, no exclusion.

The possible claims · drag each to its room
GER claims the profit it lost because the supply was late
A claim that the Contractor did not meet the agreed professional care (clause 6)
The cost of correcting a defect in delivered equipment
A claim for fraud
A claim based on Meridian's gross negligence
A clean-up claim under the environmental indemnity (clause 14)
A · General cap (16.1)
B · Environmental cap (16.2)
C · Excluded loss (16.3)
D · No cap · Protected Liabilities (16.5)
TEACHER NOTE · feedback for Ex 5.8

Answers with the reason, claim by claim. (1) Defect correction → A: an ordinary claim (and 16.4 keeps correction costs recoverable, inside the general cap). (2) Clean-up under clause 14 → B: its own cap of EUR 20,000,000. (3) Lost profit from the late supply → C: excluded by 16.3. (4) Gross negligence → D: Protected Liability. (5) Fraud → D. (6) Missing the agreed professional care → A: an ordinary breach.

Trap. A loss of profit caused by delay is excluded (16.3) but the agreed delay damages of clause 15 are recoverable (16.4). The two are not the same: delay damages are a price agreed in advance; lost profit is a loss the parties chose to exclude. Ask: why do they feel the same to a manager? Because both are “money for being late”; the contract treats one as a price and the other as a loss.

Law note (verify). D3 is governed by Italian law: an advance exclusion or limit of liability for wilful misconduct or gross negligence is not valid (Civil Code Art. 1229), which is why D3 16.5 leaves them outside every cap. For agreed delay damages the Civil Code (Art. 1382) says that the penalty limits the damages to the agreed sum unless more is expressly reserved, and a court may reduce it (Art. 1384): that is why D3 15 says that delay damages are the sole monetary remedy. D2 is governed by English law, which treats these points differently. All of these are points for a lawyer to confirm.

Ex 5.9Two clauses, one problem12 minJV · D2

Four pairs of clauses that contradict each other or chase each other. Read each pair, then answer: what happens on the day someone relies on one of them?

Part of the contractPreliminary, operative and boilerplate
Clause / headingD2 15.3 vs Annex I H.2 · NDA 5.2 vs 5.3 · D2 5.1 vs 5.2 · NDA 1.1(a) vs 1.1(b)
Why it mattersContracts fail when two clauses say different things.
TEACHER SAYS · before Ex 5.9 · ★ core

“Contracts rarely fail because a clause is missing. They fail because two clauses say different things. Four pairs. Work on your own: for each, read both clauses, answer the question and say who gains from the confusion.”

Reading rule · contra proferentem

If an ambiguity in a contract cannot be resolved in any other way, it is interpreted against the interests of the party that proposed it (non-drafting party bias). It is a last resort, and it is stronger for B2C contracts (for example under unfair contract terms rules, such as UCTA in the UK). Verify the rule in the governing law (English law; Italian Civil Code Art. 1370 for standard terms).

Indemnification (Pair 3) is a promise to pay: “Each Party agrees to indemnify the other against liabilities arising from negligence.”

Pair 1 · Which document prevails?

D2 Article 15.3

If this Agreement and Annex I conflict on a matter concerning the licence, Annex I prevails.

Annex I Section H.2

If this Annex I conflicts with the Agreement, the Agreement prevails.

GER’s liability for a defect in SeismoCore is disputed. D2 10.2 caps each party at USD 25,000,000. Annex I G.1 caps GER at the royalties PETROX paid in the previous 12 months. Which cap applies?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ 15.3 says that Annex I prevails on the licence.
✗ H.2 says that the Agreement prevails.
✓ The two rules chase each other in a circle. Each side will quote the cap that suits it, and an arbitrator (D2 13) decides after months. In the first year the royalties may be small: the difference between the caps can be enormous.
Which fix is best?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ It leaves the loop in place.
✗ It does not solve a conflict: it renames it.
✓ One rule, one place, and an order that names what prevails on what. “To the extent possible” and “equally” add more doubt, not less.

Pair 2 · How long does confidentiality last?

NDA Clause 5.2

The confidentiality obligations undertaken by the Receiving Party pursuant to Clause 2 hereof shall survive the expiry or termination of this Agreement and shall remain binding upon the Receiving Party in perpetuity.

NDA Clause 5.3

The Receiving Party’s obligations of confidentiality hereunder shall, following the termination or expiry of this Agreement, continue to bind the Receiving Party for a period of five (5) years from the date of such termination or expiry.

The NDA started on 14 February 2025 and lasts two years (5.1). On 18 March 2027, is PETROX still bound to keep the information confidential?
✗ They overlap rather than cancel: for the first five years they say the same.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ Expiry ends the term (5.1), not the duty: 5.2 and 5.3 both say that the confidentiality obligations continue.
✓ Both readings protect GER on 18 March 2027. The contradiction bites only after 14 February 2032: for ever, or finished? The real weak points in March 2027 are different (see Ex 5.10): the date of the disclosure and whether the software is covered. The fix is still one survival rule with one number.
Annex I C.1 says “the terms of the NDA apply” to the licensed technology. The NDA’s term ended on 14 February 2027. What is the risk?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ The Annex depends on the NDA for confidentiality, so its length does not help.
✗ Nothing in the documents says so.
✓ A licence of ten years (Annex I F.1) rests on an NDA that lasted two, was written for data and models (its Schedule 1) and for an evaluation purpose. Software deserves its own confidentiality clause and its own duration.

Pair 3 · Who pays when a GER engineer is injured?

D2 Article 5.1

Each Party shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the other Party… from and against any and all claims… arising out of… (a) any bodily injury to or death of any person employed by or contracted to the Indemnifying Party; and (b) any loss of or damage to the property of the Indemnifying Party; regardless of the negligence (whether sole, concurrent, gross, or otherwise)… of any Indemnitee.

D2 Article 5.2

PETROX shall indemnify, defend, and hold GER harmless from and against any and all claims… arising out of or in connection with any bodily injury to, or death of, any employee, contractor, or agent of GER or any GER Affiliate, howsoever caused.

A GER engineer is injured on the platform because of a GER mistake. Who pays under 5.1 and who under 5.2?
✗ 5.2 puts the loss on PETROX.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ 5.1 makes GER pay for GER’s people.
✓ Knock-for-knock means each Party carries the loss of its own people. 5.2 turns it into a one-way indemnity. PETROX probably did not intend that: ask the client which one is the deal.
Both clauses reach gross negligence. D3 is under Italian law and its cap clause leaves gross negligence outside the cap (16.5). D2 is under English law (13.1). What should a reviewer do?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ It depends on the governing law.
✗ 5.1 is the commercial deal. Fix it, do not delete it.
✓ Two laws in one project is itself a finding. The safe habit is a carve-out for fraud, wilful misconduct and gross negligence in every cap, exclusion and indemnity, then a lawyer decides what the governing law allows.

Pair 4 · Two definitions that chase each other (NDA 1.1)

NDA Clause 1.1(a) · Affiliate

“Affiliate” shall mean any entity that, directly or indirectly, controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with a Party, whereby ‘control’ shall be construed in accordance with the provisions of sub-clause 1.1(a)(i) hereof, and the definition of ‘Affiliate’ shall be deemed to include any Subsidiary as defined in sub-clause 1.1(b) below;

NDA Clause 1.1(b) · Subsidiary

“Subsidiary” shall mean any entity that constitutes a controlled Affiliate of a Party pursuant to the definition set out in sub-clause 1.1(a) above and the control thresholds specified therein;

Why is this a circular definition?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ Repeating a word is not the problem: the loop between the two definitions is.
✗ They are not short; they are empty in the middle.
✓ To know what an Affiliate is you must know what a Subsidiary is, and to know what a Subsidiary is you must know what an Affiliate is. The reader goes round in a circle and never reaches a rule.
The way out of the circle would be a test for “control”. Where does the NDA give it?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ Schedule 1 describes the Confidential Information, not control.
✗ Clause 5 deals with duration.
✓ Two promises of a test and no test. This matters because “Representatives” (1.1(d)) include any Subsidiary or Affiliate: PETROX may share GER’s information with them, and nobody can say who they are.
TEACHER NOTE · Pair 4

Fix (say it simply). One definition only, with a real test: “Affiliate means any entity that controls, is controlled by or is under common control with a Party. An entity controls another if it holds more than 50% of the votes or has the power to direct its management.” Delete “Subsidiary” if you do not need it, or define it by a different word (for example “a company in which a Party holds more than 50% of the votes”). The percentage is a drafting choice for the client, not a legal rule: ask.

Why it matters. The cross-reference to “1.1(a)(i)” also teaches a habit: always click every cross-reference in the final draft.

FEEDBACK · Ex 5.9 · for you only

What happens on the day someone relies on one of them? (Pairs 1 to 3) Nothing automatic: no clause wins by itself. Each side quotes the clause that suits it, the other quotes the opposite, and the argument is about intention. A tribunal reads the contract as a whole, looks at the order of precedence if there is one (D2 has one only for D2 against Annex I, and Annex I answers the opposite), and then at what a reasonable party would have understood. Under Italian law the interpretation rules are Art. 1362 (common intention), Art. 1363 (clauses read together) and, as a last resort for standard terms, Art. 1370 (against the one who wrote them); English law reads the words objectively in their context (verify both).

Which document prevails? Pair 1: D2 15.3 says Annex I; Annex I H.2 says D2. Neither wins on its face. The tribunal will ask which clause is more specific and which one the parties meant for the licence. That is a gamble nobody wants.

Is arbitration the only solution? No, and it is the last one. (1) The parties may fix the text together by a signed amendment (D2 15.2). (2) They can negotiate: D3 has 20 Business Days of escalation before the courts. (3) For the Joint Account, D2 13.3 allows an independent accounting expert. (4) For urgent matters, D2 13.3 allows urgent court relief. (5) Only after that, ICC arbitration, seat London (D2 13.2): months of time and cost. The best remedy is prevention: one rule, one place.

POSSIBLE QUESTIONS · ANSWERS

Q: Is a contradiction always a drafting mistake? A: Often it is two drafters, two templates, or an old clause nobody removed. Sometimes it is a negotiation that ended without cleaning the text. Either way the reviewer reports it and asks the client which version is the deal.

Q: Does a longer or more detailed clause win? A: Not by itself. A tribunal looks first for an order of precedence in the contract, then at the more specific clause, then at the purpose. A written order of precedence is the cheapest insurance.

Q: Who gains from the confusion? A: The party that is in a hurry to claim. A clear clause protects both parties; an unclear one rewards the one with the better lawyers.

D. Breaches and remedies

TRANSITION

"Contracts exist for the day something goes wrong. Same event, four documents. Let us follow one fact: on a date in March 2027, GER learns that PETROX gave SeismoCore specifications to a third party. What can GER do? Which clause tells it how?"

Reading before the ladder · remedies

Remedies for breach of an NDA

The remedies for breach are monetary damages and/or injunctive relief.

Monetary relief consists of compensation. Injunctive relief is a court order telling the other party to stop the disclosure.

This is where the penalties or consequences of violation are outlined. You can sue for damages if there is a breach; if you only want them to stop using or giving out your information, you can ask for injunctive relief.

Model clause: “Remedies. Each party’s obligations in this Agreement are necessary and reasonable to protect the other party and the other party’s business. Because monetary damages would be inadequate to compensate the other party, and because a breach or threatened breach will cause irreparable injury to the other party, that party may seek injunctive relief to prevent the breach, the threatened breach or the continuation of a breach without need to prove actual damages.”

Remedies and damages · what the law gives

The fundamental purpose of remedies in commercial agreements is not to punish but, if possible, to put the non-breaching party in the position it would have been in had there been no breach. There are two main categories: equitable remedies (actions, ordered by a court) and legal remedies (financial compensation).

Equitable remedies: specific performance (a person is ordered to deliver a unique thing, such as land or a unique painting); injunction (a court order to stop doing something, such as competing in violation of a non-compete); restitution (putting the parties back in the position they were in before the contract).

Legal remedies are known as damages. Compensatory: reimburse the loss suffered. Consequential: the foreseeable consequences of the breach. Incidental: the costs of keeping more damages from occurring. Nominal: awarded if the amount cannot be shown or there is no actual damage. Liquidated: agreed in advance where the actual amount is hard to ascertain, allowed if not a penalty. Punitive: sometimes allowed for an outrageous tort.

GER mainly wants PETROX to stop disclosing SeismoCore specifications today. Which remedy is the closest?
✗ Liquidated damages are a sum agreed in advance.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ Nominal damages are a token sum when no loss can be shown.
✓ Money does not undo a disclosure; an injunction stops it. The D4 demand “cease and desist” asks for the same thing without a court. D2 13.3 allows urgent court relief.
D3 clause 15 sets delay damages in advance, with a daily rate and a cap. Which type of damages are they?
✗ Restitution returns what was received.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ Punitive damages punish; delay damages compensate.
✓ They are a price fixed in advance, not a punishment. Under Italian law a similar clause is a “clausola penale” (Civil Code Arts. 1382–1384, verify), which a court may reduce if it is excessive.

SAY · FEEDBACK · the breach ladder

Debrief (3 minutes). "Where does the NDA fit?" It is step 1: the breach. "Where does Annex I come in?" C.1 brings the NDA into the licence; F.2 allows suspension for non-payment, not for disclosure. "What is the weakest link?" The notice: if it lacks a date or a cure period, the ladder collapses at step 2.

Correct answer to “Is the NDA still alive on 18 March 2027?” The two-year term ended on 14 February 2027 (5.1), but the confidentiality duty did not. Clause 5.2 says it survives “in perpetuity”; 5.3 says five years from the end, that is until 14 February 2032. On 18 March 2027 both clauses say that PETROX is still bound. The contradiction matters only after February 2032. So the NDA as a contract has ended, but PETROX’s duty not to disclose has not.

What can still go wrong for GER. (1) The date of the disclosure. The letter gives none. If the disclosure happened before 14 February 2027 the NDA was fully in force; if after, GER relies on the survival clauses. Either way GER needs the date. (2) Is the software covered? The NDA’s Schedule 1 lists data and models, not SeismoCore; Annex I C.1 only says that “the terms of the NDA apply”, and the NDA was written for an evaluation purpose and a short term. GER should rely on Annex I C.1 and on D2, and the weak fit is a finding. (3) The NDA has no governing-law clause, so the law that reads 5.2 and 5.3 is itself uncertain.

Legal notes (verify). Under English law there is no default term for a confidentiality duty: it is what the contract says. An indefinite duty is not automatically void, but a court is unlikely to enforce it for information that is no longer confidential. If two clauses really conflict, reading against the drafter (contra proferentem) is a last resort. Under Italian law, Arts. 1362–1363 Civil Code first (common intention; clauses read together); Art. 1370 (against the author) applies to standard terms and only subsidiarily. Sources consulted: Orrick FAQ on NDA duration; Ashurst quickguide on confidentiality; avvocato.it on Art. 1370.

① Pick a tool. ② Click words, or drag across them. Click again with the same tool to undo. Everyone works differently: there is no single right way to mark.

GLOBAL ENERGY RESOURCES S.p.A., Via Cesare Pavese 14, 20138 Milan (MI), Italy
Date: 18 March 2027
By Registered Post and Electronic Mail STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL

SENDINGhow the letter travels

What to say. The words “By Registered Post and Electronic Mail” are not plain English because they are capitalised as if they were a title, and because they hide a question: does this way of sending satisfy the contract? D2 14.1 asks for a notice to be sent by courier as well, and D2 14.2 sets when email counts as received. The letter says nothing of courier, nor of a date of receipt. “Strictly private and confidential” is fine but says nothing the envelope does not.
Plain wording: “By courier and by email (notice under Clause 11.2 of the Joint Development and Production Agreement)”.


The Board of Directors, PETROX INTERNATIONAL LIMITED, 88 Cannon Street, London EC4N 6JJ, United Kingdom

ADDRESSEEwho receives it

What to say. “The Board of Directors” sounds important, but D2 14.3 names the Company Secretary as the person who receives notices. A letter to the wrong person can be argued not to have been properly given, and then the cure period never starts. In a notice, importance of the addressee matters less than the address the contract names. Ask: who would open this envelope in London?


Dear Sirs,

SALUTATIONhow we greet

What to say. “Dear Sirs” is dated and assumes everybody is a man; a company is not a “Sir”. Use “Dear Sir or Madam” or, better, the name of the Company Secretary. The salutation and the closing go together: “Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully”; with a name, “Dear Ms Rossi … Yours sincerely”.


Re: NOTICE OF MATERIAL BREACH AND DEMAND FOR IMMEDIATE REMEDIATION PURSUANT TO CLAUSE 2 OF THE NON-DISCLOSURE AGREEMENT DATED 14 FEBRUARY 2025 AND ARTICLE C.1 OF ANNEX I TO THE JOINT DEVELOPMENT AND PRODUCTION AGREEMENT DATED 30 JUNE 2025 (THE 'RELEVANT AGREEMENTS')

LABELwhat the letter is about

What to say. The Re line is the label of the letter, and this label has four problems. (1) It is in capitals, which is harder to read. (2) The numbers are inexact: the NDA obligation is in Clause 2.1 and Annex I uses “Section C.1”, not “Article”. (3) It defines “Relevant Agreements” inside a heading: a definition belongs in the text. (4) It does not say that this is a notice under D2 Clause 11.2, which 11.2 requires. “Demand for immediate remediation” also promises something the letter never gives: there is no date.


We write to you heretofore and hereinafter in respect of certain matters which have recently come to the attention of Global Energy Resources S.p.A. (hereinafter referred to as 'GER' or 'our client' or 'the Aggrieved Party') concerning the actions, omissions, and conduct of PETROX International Limited (hereinafter referred to as 'PETROX' or 'you' or 'your organisation' or 'the Defaulting Party') which, GER avers and contends, constitute a material breach of the Relevant Agreements.

OPENINGthe first paragraph

What to say. “Heretofore and hereinafter” mean “until now and from now on”: here they mean nothing, delete them. “Concerning the actions, omissions, and conduct of” is bloat: say “about”. “Avers and contends” are two old words for “states”. GER receives three names (“GER”, “our client”, “the Aggrieved Party”), and “our client” is wrong because GER is writing for itself; PETROX gets four names. “The Defaulting Party” is a trap: under D2 that name belongs to a party that has already reached an Event of Default, which is exactly what the letter must still prove. One name each: GER and PETROX.


It has come to the attention of GER that, notwithstanding the express obligations of confidentiality… PETROX has, without the knowledge, consent, or authorisation of GER, and in direct and flagrant contravention of its obligations thereunder, disclosed, divulged, communicated, or caused to be disclosed certain Confidential Information, to wit, aspects of the SeismoCoreTM Licensed Technology specifications and certain Derived Data outputs, to third parties, the identity of whom is as yet not fully known to GER.

THE FACTSwhat happened

What to say. This is the paragraph that must carry the proof, and it carries none: no date, no recipient, no document. Four verbs for one idea (“disclosed, divulged, communicated, or caused to be disclosed”): one is enough. “Without the knowledge, consent, or authorisation… in direct and flagrant contravention” piles emotion on a fact. “To wit” means “namely”. “Aspects of” is vague: which specifications? And “the identity of whom is as yet not fully known to GER” admits a weakness and is not good grammar. Say what GER knows and reserve the right to add details.


GER hereby puts PETROX on formal notice that the aforesaid conduct constitutes, in GER's considered opinion and on legal advice, a material breach of the Relevant Agreements, and GER hereby demands forthwith, and not later than such time as may be reasonably practicable in all the circumstances, that PETROX:

THE DEMANDwhat GER asks, and by when

What to say. “In GER’s considered opinion and on legal advice” adds nothing: a party does not need to say that it has taken advice, and mentioning it can raise questions about what was said (verify the position on privilege). The key words are “forthwith, and not later than such time as may be reasonably practicable in all the circumstances”: three vague time words and no date. The cure period under D2 11.1(b) needs a number: 30 days after the notice. Ask: from which day does PETROX’s time run? Nobody can say.


Labels to remember

PASSIVE actor missing or last · SHALL duty, future or permission? · DOUBLET two or more words for one idea · BLOAT words that add nothing · NEGATIVE stacked not/no · VAGUE no measurable standard · OLD WORD hereinafter, herein · HIDDEN VERB the action buried in a noun

💡 SUGGESTED DRAFTING · when you have organised your ideas, click here (or press Check) to open the clause in plain English.
SUGGESTED DRAFTING · plain English, same purpose. Use it as feedback on how you organised the clause.

Re: Notice of material breach of the NDA dated 14 February 2025 (Clause 2.1) and of Annex I to the Joint Development and Production Agreement dated 30 June 2025 (Section C.1). This is a notice under Clause 11.2 of the Joint Development and Production Agreement.

1. This notice. GER gives formal notice that PETROX has materially breached the agreements above. This letter states the breach, GER's demands, the cure period and the consequence of not complying.

2. The breach. On or around [SPECIFIC DATE], PETROX disclosed specifications of GER's SeismoCore software (version 7.2) and processed seismic data from Blocks 14/06 and 15/07 to [NAME OR DESCRIPTION OF THIRD PARTY], without GER's prior written consent. This breached: (a) Clause 2.1 of the NDA (no disclosure without GER's prior written consent); and (b) Section C.1 of Annex I (the Licensed Technology is Confidential Information under the NDA).

Sending and signing. Address the notice to the Company Secretary of PETROX at the address in D2 Article 14.3. State that it is sent by courier and by email (Article 14.1). Sign with a name, a title and the authority to sign. Start “Dear Sir or Madam” and close “Yours faithfully”: no “Dear Sirs”. Do not write “on legal advice”.

Seven things now present: a date, the clause numbers, the facts, a defined third party, the Article 11.2 statement, a correct way of sending and addressing, and no “forthwith”. The date and the third party are brackets: GER must fill them with facts it can prove.

Tick the true statements about the D4 letter.
✓ Seven are true. The letter names no third party (it says the identity is “not fully known”), it fixes no cure period (“a period to be determined by GER”) and the old words are legalese. The last point matters most: a notice that is sent or addressed the wrong way may not start the clock.
TEACHER NOTE

Features of a good notice. (1) A specific breach date: it fixes the start of the clock. (2) Specific clause references: a court must find the exact obligation without reading the whole contract. (3) Numbered, specific demands: each demand can be enforced alone. (4) A specific cure deadline: “a reasonable time” never starts the clock. (5) One elected remedy for non-compliance. (6) A targeted reservation of damages for past losses. (7) Sent and addressed as the contract says.

Real Horizon point: D2 11.2 requires a statement that the notice is given under 11.2, so the model adds it. Also: “identity not fully known” admits a weakness. Say what GER knows and reserve the right to add particulars.

CLAUSE PROFILE · D4 · Letter of Notice (opening paragraphs)

What it is and its job. The enforcement document: it tells PETROX what it did wrong, what GER wants, by when, and what happens if PETROX does not comply.

What it should contain. A date and the facts of the breach; the clause numbers; demands, numbered and measurable; a cure date; the remedy GER chooses if the demands are not met; a short reservation of damages; and the formalities of D2 Art. 14 and 11.2.

Why it matters in Project Horizon. D4 is the end of the story: it works only if the NDA, Annex I and D2 gave GER the right to complain and a way to do it. A weak letter wastes a strong contract.

How it relates to the other contracts. The letter relies on NDA 2.1 and Annex I C.1 (the breach), on D2 11.1(b) and 11.2 (the cure and notice rules) and on D2 14 (how the notice is sent). It is the one place where all three meet.

SHAPING THE EXERCISE · what to ask while they organize

Check the three answers: GER must prove the date, the clause and the facts; the letter is written for PETROX first and for a judge or arbitrator second; the three changes that matter most are the date, the cure date and one remedy.

Extra question: Why does the letter say “our client” when GER writes for itself? (a template copied from a law firm).

Extra question: What happens if PETROX answers that it never received the letter? (the sending rules of D2 14 decide: courier and email, to the named person).

TRANSITION

The first paragraphs are a diagnosis. Now the part that matters most: the demands, the deadline and the consequence.

Original · D4 demands

(i) Cease and desist forthwith from any further disclosure, use, or exploitation of the Confidential Information or the Licensed Technology for any purpose other than as expressly permitted under the Relevant Agreements;

(ii) Provide GER with a full and unqualified written account, verified by statutory declaration, of all disclosures made, to whom, and in what form, within a period to be determined by GER;

(iii) Procure the immediate return or certified destruction of all Confidential Information disclosed to any third party, to the extent that such procurement is within PETROX’s power;

(iv) Pay to GER such damages, losses, costs, and expenses as GER may suffer or incur as a consequence of the said breach, the quantum of which is expressly reserved.

GER further reserves all rights and remedies available to it at law or in equity, including but not limited to the right to seek injunctive relief, specific performance, and damages for breach of contract. Should PETROX fail to comply with the demands herein within a reasonable time, GER reserves the right to take such further steps, including the commencement of legal proceedings, as it may deem necessary and appropriate in the circumstances.

Plain English · model demands

3. GER’s demands. PETROX must, by [CURE DATE: 30 days after this notice, as in D2 Clause 11.1(b)]:

3.1 stop at once all further disclosure or use of the Confidential Information and the Licensed Technology;

3.2 give GER a written account, verified by a statutory declaration, that states: (a) every third party to which Confidential Information was disclosed; (b) the date, form and scope of each disclosure; and (c) each third party’s current contact details;

3.3 obtain the return or certified destruction of all Confidential Information from every third party named under 3.2; and

3.4 give GER written proof that demands 3.1 to 3.3 have been fully met.

4. If PETROX does not comply. If PETROX does not meet all the demands in Clause 3 by [CURE DATE], an Event of Default will exist under Clause 11.1(b) of the Joint Development and Production Agreement, and GER may end that Agreement and Annex I by written notice under Clause 11.3.

5. Reservation. GER reserves its right to claim damages for the losses it has already suffered as a result of the breach in Clause 2, whether or not PETROX meets the demands in Clause 3.

INSTRUCTOR NOTE · summary and check, right after the two columns

Summary note (say it after they have read both columns). The original contains four demands, a reservation of everything and a threat without a date. Demand (i) stop; (ii) give an account, “within a period to be determined by GER”; (iii) return or destroy; (iv) pay damages of an amount nobody knows. Then GER reserves “all rights and remedies” and says that if PETROX does not comply “within a reasonable time” it may do “such further steps” as it likes. Nothing says by when, and nothing says what exactly will happen.

Check that they got it. Ask three quick questions and wait for answers: (1) How many demands are there, and which one cannot be fulfilled? (four; the fourth, because the amount is unknown) (2) What date should be in each demand? (one cure date, 30 days after the notice) (3) What does GER really want to be able to say at the end? (that an Event of Default exists and that it may end D2).

The model in one line. One cure date, numbered demands that PETROX can do, one clear consequence, and damages reserved separately.

In the original, from which day does PETROX’s time to comply start to run?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ The letter does not say so.
✗ The 30 days come from D2 11.1(b), but the letter does not state them.
✓ With no date, no cure period starts. D2 11.1(b) needs a notice that states the cure period; without it GER cannot safely say that an Event of Default exists or terminate. The model gives one cure date.
Demand (iv) asks PETROX to pay damages “the quantum of which is expressly reserved”. What is the problem?
✗ The problem is not the size but that there is no amount.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ A reservation is fine; a demand of unknown amount is not.
✓ A demand must be something the other side can do by a date. The model reserves damages for past losses (clause 5) and does not ask for payment now.
The original reserves every right and also threatens proceedings. Why does the model choose one remedy?
✗ No court requires it; it is good drafting.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ GER keeps its rights; the letter simply chooses.
✓ The model states one consequence (an Event of Default and the right to end D2) plus a targeted reservation of damages for past losses.
The model says GER “may end” D2, not “will end” it. Why?
✗ It is about commitment, not politeness.
✗ The difference is the point.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✓ must = duty, may = right, will = a future step of a procedure. A notice that says “will” can be read as a commitment. Ending a 60/40 joint venture is a big decision: keep it optional.
FEEDBACK · Ex 5.12

Feedback (2 minutes). A good letter answers four questions for the reader: what happened, what do you want, by when, and what happens if you do not. The original answers the first one in a vague way and none of the others with a date. Under D2 11.1(b) and 11.2 the notice is the document that starts the 30 days; if it does not, GER cannot treat PETROX as in default. The model shows how little is needed: a date in brackets, three or four verbs in the active voice, and one sentence of consequence.

POSSIBLE QUESTIONS · ANSWERS

Q: What if PETROX replies that it needs more time? A: The 30 days are the contractual cure period. GER may agree to extend in writing, but only knowingly: a casual email extending the time can later be used to say GER waived the deadline (see D2 15.5, no waiver).

Q: What if PETROX says the information is already public? A: That is an exception under NDA Clause 4 (public domain). The letter should state the facts precisely enough for PETROX to answer one by one.

Q: Why 30 days and not a shorter period? A: Because D2 11.1(b) gives 30 days to cure and the letter relies on D2. A shorter period in the letter could be challenged.

Q: Can GER demand the return of information held by a third party? A: Only “to the extent within PETROX’s power”: PETROX cannot be forced to do what it cannot do. The model says “obtain the return or destruction”: ask whether PETROX can.

Q: Why must the notice also go by courier? A: D2 14.1: a notice under 11.2 or of termination must also be sent by courier, not only by email.

E. Case study and standard wording

TRANSITION

“Companies keep a standard version of their favourite clauses. In our course material this is called the standard wording: the clause as it should read. We use it in two ways: as a case study of something that went wrong, and as a model to compare with raw wording.”

NOTE ON THE STANDARD WORDING

Source of the “standard wording”. It is course material, not a real company template: every number (48 hours, 180 days, 2 hours) is a drafting choice that the parties may negotiate. Verify against your own company’s templates before using any of it outside this course.

Ex 5.13Case study · who owns what PETROX produces?10 minJV · D2

A case study. Read the story, assemble the clues into the rules the contract needs, then compare with D2 Article 4 and answer the questions.

Part of the contractOperative · intellectual property and data
Clause / headingD2 Article 4 · Derived Data
Why it mattersThe data is the value of the project: who owns what must be clear.
TEACHER SAYS · before Ex 5.13 · ★ core · individual work

“Case study. Work on your own. First read the story. Under it there are nine clues: drag each one to the rule it belongs to. Solve the case before you open Article 4. When you press Check, the clause that was really written appears, and you will see that your clues are its sentences. Then compare the original with the clearer version and answer the three questions. The point is not the wording: it is the money that depends on it.”

The case · who owns what PETROX produces?

Year 1. PETROX runs GER’s SeismoCore software on seismic data from the Contract Area and produces three kinds of results: raw processing outputs, reservoir models and, one day, a completely new method to predict pressure.

Year 2. A bank offers to finance the project if PETROX hands over its reservoir model. GER objects: “the software is ours, and so are half the results.” PETROX answers: “the results are ours.” The contract has to give an answer. What must it say?

Your job. Five rules answer the case. Drag each clue to the rule it supports; two clues do not belong in the deal.

A completely new method nobody had before: GER 70% and PETROX 30%
Everything PETROX creates by running the software needs one single name
PETROX says it is a model; GER says it is a new method
PETROX may sell a copy of SeismoCore to the bank
PETROX may run SeismoCore but never takes the software home
Raw seismic processing outputs: GER 60% and PETROX 40%
Everything PETROX produces is split in equal halves
Reservoir models: 50% each
The bank asks PETROX for a copy of the reservoir model
Rule 1 · who owns the software
Rule 2 · one name for what PETROX produces
Rule 3 · who owns what share
Rule 4 · who may license to others
Rule 5 · who decides when the category is unclear
Not part of the deal (or a trap)
Case solved: this is Article 4.
  • Rule 1 = 4.1. GER owns the Intellectual Property in the Licensed Technology; nothing is transferred to PETROX.
  • Rule 2 = the definition in 4.2. “Derived Data” is the single name for everything PETROX creates when it uses the software.
  • Rule 3 = the three splits in 4.2: 60/40, 50/50 and 70/30.
  • Rule 4 = 4.3 (a client decision). A Party may license Derived Data to a third party only with the other Party’s written consent: the bank’s request is answered here.
  • Rule 5 = 4.4 (a client decision). An independent technical expert decides which category applies.
  • The trap = the word “equal”. The original also says that everything is owned “in equal undivided shares”, which contradicts the three splits. That is the clause GER’s lawyers found.

Your clues are the sentences of the clause. Now see how the original wrote them.

Original · D2 Article 4

4.1 All Intellectual Property rights in and to the Licensed Technology shall remain vested in and the absolute property of GER, and nothing in this Agreement shall be construed to transfer, assign, or convey any Intellectual Property right to PETROX.

4.2 All data, results, interpretations, and derivative works created by PETROX in the course of using the Licensed Technology (‘Derived Data’) shall be jointly owned by the Parties in equal undivided shares, subject to the following allocation: (a) Derived Data relating to raw seismic processing outputs shall be owned sixty percent (60%) by GER and forty percent (40%) by PETROX; (b) Derived Data relating to reservoir modelling and characterisation shall be owned fifty percent (50%) by each Party; (c) Derived Data that constitutes a novel discovery, methodology, or process (‘New IP’) shall be owned seventy percent (70%) by GER and thirty percent (30%) by PETROX.

Plain English · same deal, one rule

4.1 GER owns all Intellectual Property rights in the Licensed Technology. Nothing in this Agreement transfers any of those rights to PETROX.

4.2 “Derived Data” means all data, results, interpretations and derivative works that PETROX creates when it uses the Licensed Technology. The Parties own Derived Data in these shares: (a) raw seismic processing outputs: GER 60% and PETROX 40%; (b) reservoir modelling and characterisation: 50% each; (c) a novel discovery, method or process (“New IP”): GER 70% and PETROX 30%.

4.3 [Client decision] Each Party may use Derived Data for its own internal operational and reporting purposes. A Party may license Derived Data to a third party only with the other Party’s written consent.

4.4 [Client decision] If the Parties disagree about which category applies, an independent technical expert chosen by both decides.

In the original, what share of the Derived Data does PETROX own?
✗ The word “equal” still creates the doubt.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ (a) to (c) give other shares.
✓ The heading rule (equal) and the list (60/40, 50/50, 70/30) contradict each other. Each side will quote the one that suits it, and a court has to choose. The plain version keeps the three splits, which are the commercial deal, and deletes the word “equal”.
A reservoir model contains a new method to predict pressure. Is it category (b) modelling or (c) New IP, and why does it matter?
✗ The shares are different: 50% and 30%.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ Nothing in the clause says (b) wins.
✓ The categories overlap. The plain version adds an independent expert (4.4, a client decision) so that a dispute about the category has an answer.
PETROX wants to license a reservoir model to a third party. Does the original allow it?
✗ Ownership does not by itself answer who may license.
✗ GER owns the technology, not the Derived Data.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✓ Joint ownership without a rule on use and licensing is a classic source of disputes. The default rules depend on the governing law (English law here): verify before advising.
CLAUSE PROFILE · D2 Article 4 (IP and data ownership)

What it is and its job. Says who owns the technology and who owns what PETROX produces with it.

What it should contain. The owner of the technology (GER); a definition of Derived Data; who owns each kind of data and in which share; the rights of use and licensing for joint owners; and what happens on termination.

Why it matters in Project Horizon. The data is the value of the project. An ownership clause that contradicts itself is what gets argued over after a discovery.

How it relates to the other contracts. Annex I A.1 grants only use rights, so 4.1 must agree: GER keeps the technology. NDA 2.1 protects the data while it is confidential. D2 11.4 says what survives termination (Articles 5, 10, 13): ownership of Derived Data is not on the list.

SHAPING THE EXERCISE · what to ask while they organize

Ask: How many ownership rules do you find in 4.2? (two: equal and unequal).

Ask: Which one is the deal? (the percentages).

Ask: What does the clause not say that a lawyer would ask? (use and licensing by joint owners; survival).

TRANSITION

A case study shows one clause that went wrong. Standard wording shows the whole clause done right.

Ex 5.14Standard wording · force majeure and notices12 minJV · D2

A case study. Read the story, assemble the clues, see how they become the force majeure clause, answer the questions. Then fix the notice clause.

Part of the contractBoilerplate · force majeure and notices
Clause / headingD2 Article 6 · D3 clause 21 · NDA 8.4 · D2 14 · D3 22
Why it mattersBoilerplate looks standard, but it decides the day something goes wrong.
TEACHER SAYS · before Ex 5.14 · individual work

“Two boilerplates that nobody reads until the day they are needed: force majeure and notices. Work on your own. First the case: read the story and drag the clues to the rule they belong to. Press Check and you will see the clause they build. Then compare with the original and answer: what does each missing sentence cost?”

A force majeure clause answers four questions

In case of what? (which events count: 6.1) · When? (how fast must the affected party tell the other: 6.3) · How? (what it must do: describe the event and try to overcome it) · What then? (what is excused, and what happens if it lasts too long: 6.2 and 6.4).

Model sentence: “No party is liable or responsible to the other, nor is it in breach, for a delay in performance when and to the extent the failure or delay is caused by acts beyond the party’s control.”

The case · the storm, the strike and the 14 months

March. A storm closes the port that supplies the platform. The work stops. PETROX tells GER about it 40 days later.

April. A bank strike delays PETROX’s cash-call payment by a month. PETROX says: “force majeure”.

The next year. Port damage keeps the work stopped for 14 months. Nobody can say when it will restart. What should the contract say in each situation?

Your job. Drag each clue to the rule it supports. Two clues describe wording that the clause should not have.

The bank strike does not excuse a payment already due
Only an event beyond reasonable control that could not be prevented with reasonable care counts
“As soon as reasonably practicable” is enough notice
The list stays open: “and any other events of a similar nature”
PETROX must tell GER within 48 hours, describe the event and its expected duration and try to overcome it
The list of events is closed: fire, flood, earthquake, epidemic, war, terrorism, civil disturbance, government action that prevents performance
After 180 days either Party may end the agreement by written notice
The stopped work is excused only for as long as the storm prevents or delays it
Rule 1 · what counts as force majeure (6.1)
Rule 2 · what is excused and what is not (6.2)
Rule 3 · how to tell the other side (6.3)
Rule 4 · when it goes on too long (6.4)
Wording the clause should not have
Case solved: this is the force majeure clause.
  • 6.1 defines the event with a closed list and a test (beyond reasonable control, not preventable with reasonable diligence).
  • 6.2 excuses only what the event really prevents, and never a payment already due: the bank strike does not help PETROX.
  • 6.3 turns “as soon as reasonably practicable” into 48 hours plus content: what happened, how long, what PETROX will do. The 40 days of the story would have been a clear breach of this rule.
  • 6.4 answers the 14 months: after 180 days either Party can end the agreement. The original had no long-stop, so both were stuck.

The two wrong clues are exactly the original’s wording: an open list and a notice with no date. Now compare the original and the clearer version.

Original · D2 Article 6

6.1 “Force Majeure Event” shall mean any event or circumstance beyond the reasonable control of the affected Party, including without limitation: acts of God, fires, floods, earthquakes, epidemics, wars (whether declared or undeclared), acts of terrorism, civil disturbances, sabotage, government actions, embargoes, blockades, labour disputes, strikes, and any other events of a similar nature or character.

6.2 If a Force Majeure Event occurs, the affected Party shall be relieved of its obligations under this Agreement to the extent that performance of such obligations is prevented or delayed by the Force Majeure Event.

6.3 The affected Party shall give notice of the Force Majeure Event to the other Party as soon as reasonably practicable.

Plain English · course standard (verify the numbers)

6.1 A “Force Majeure Event” is an event beyond the reasonable control of the affected Party that it could not have prevented or overcome with reasonable diligence. It is limited to: fire, flood, earthquake, epidemic, war, terrorism, civil disturbance, and government action that prevents performance.

6.2 The affected Party is relieved of an obligation only to the extent that the event prevents or delays it. The event does not excuse a payment that is already due.

6.3 The affected Party must notify the other Party within 48 hours after it becomes aware of the event, describe the event and its expected duration, and use all reasonable efforts to overcome it.

6.4 If the event continues for more than 180 days, either Party may end this Agreement by written notice.

PETROX tells GER about a flood 40 days after it began. Under the original 6.3, can GER object?
✗ Clause 6.3 does require notice, but without a date.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ The clause does not say what is too late.
✓ Without a deadline nobody can say when the notice was late. The plain version fixes 48 hours; the number is a drafting choice (course standard, verify it).
A force majeure event lasts 14 months. What does the original allow?
✗ No such right appears in Article 6.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ No such right appears in Article 6.
✓ The original has no right to end after a long event. The plain version adds one after 180 days (course standard, verify). D3 clause 21 uses 90 days for a Call-Off.
A bank strike delays PETROX’s cash-call payment by a month. Does the original 6.2 excuse the payment?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ The original does not say so.
✗ The original gives GER no such power.
✓ The plain version excludes payments already due, as D3 clause 21 does (“Payment for completed performance is not excused”). Note that “labour disputes” and “strikes” are on the original list.
D2 2.1 says the licence applies “save where the provisions of Article 7 (Force Majeure) shall apply”. What is Article 7?
✗ Force majeure is Article 6.
✗ Notices are Article 14.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✓ A wrong cross-reference leaves open whether force majeure relief reaches the licence at all. Always check the number against the text.

Notices · raw wording and its fix

What a notice clause must state

How notices must be given: in writing, hand-delivered, by registered post or courier. For electronic notices: whether a confirmation of delivery must be sent at once. When a notice counts as received. Business days: if you use them, define them. To whom: a named person, with an address.

Why notices matter · a Friday at 18:00

A notice is the message that starts a clock: the cure period, the time to answer, the time to pay. If the message does not arrive in the way the contract says, the clock does not start. Story. GER emails a breach notice on Friday at 18:00 to a general inbox. PETROX says it saw it on Monday. A second notice is faxed to a number that no longer works. A third goes to “The Board” instead of the Company Secretary. Which of the three starts the 30 days? The answer depends on one thing only: what the notices clause says. Read the raw wording below and fix it.

NDA 8.4 (raw)

Any notice… shall be in writing and shall be deemed to have been duly given if delivered personally, or sent by registered post or nationally recognised courier service, or by facsimile transmission with written confirmation, to the address set forth in the preamble hereof…

Problem in 8.4Fix from the standard
Fax is allowed but email is not, and nothing says when email counts as received
The address is "set forth in the preamble hereof": nobody is named
Nothing says what happens if a party moves office
Only the receiving party sees the notice; its lawyers may not
The course standard says an email notice counts as received 2 hours after sending, if sent before 17:00 on a Business Day. Why not 24 hours?
✗ It is not illegal: it is a commercial choice.
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ Email can fail. That is why the sender keeps a delivery receipt.
✓ In a breach situation, a cure period is running: a 22-hour gap can matter. With parties in different time zones, send within the recipient's business hours or the "next Business Day" rule applies. (Course standard: verify.)
TEACHER NOTE

Compare: D2 Art. 14.2 already uses a rule of this kind: email counts as received "on the next Business Day after sending, unless the sender receives a delivery-failure message". D3 clause 22 says notices "take effect on confirmed receipt". Three documents, three rules for the same thing: a mismatch to flag in the Stitch Test.

FEEDBACK · what happens if…

What happens if… (feedback, one case at a time).

…the notice goes only by email and the clause allows only post, courier and fax? PETROX can say it was never validly given. The cure period may not start. Fix: list email, and say when it counts as received.

…it is sent on Friday at 18:00? With a 2-hour rule that applies only before 17:00 on a Business Day, it counts as received on the next Business Day. Without such a rule, each side argues its own time.

…it goes to the wrong person? The clause names an addressee for a reason. A notice to the Board instead of the Company Secretary invites the argument that it was not received by the right person. Fix: name the addressee, with title and email.

…PETROX has moved office and did not tell GER? If the clause has no change-of-details rule, GER cannot know where to send; if it has one, a notice to the old address counts. Fix: a short clause on how to change details.

…the three documents have three rules? D2 14.2, D3 clause 22 and NDA 8.4 each say something different about when a notice is received. In a project that uses all three, the same letter can be received at three different moments. Flag it and align the rules.

POSSIBLE QUESTIONS · ANSWERS

Q: Is "including without limitation" always a problem? A: In force majeure it opens the list to events nobody foresaw, which may be what the party relying on it wants. The standard prefers a closed list. Which is better depends on whose side you are on.

Q: Is 180 days right for everyone? A: No. It is a number from the course standard for upstream oil and gas. Parties negotiate it.

A. Negotiation language

TRANSITION

"We negotiate with the same words we draft with, but spoken and softer. In a contract we write must; at the table we say would, could and if. Five minutes of sorting, then a table you can keep."

Ex 6.1What is this sentence doing?8 minFRAMEWORK · D3

Eight sentences from a negotiation. Drag each one to the function it performs.

TEACHER SAYS · before Ex 6.1

"Six functions: propose, set a condition, refuse politely, concede, ask for clarification, summarise. Eight sentences. Drag each one."

We are prepared to move on the notice period.
Could you explain why 60 days is not enough for you?
I am afraid we cannot agree to unlimited liability.
Would you consider a rate of EUR 25,000 a day?
We would like to propose a cap of 125% of the Call-Off price.
We could accept that, provided the cap also covers defect costs.
If you accept a minimum of EUR 11 million, we will accept 90 days' notice.
So, to confirm: 100% of the price, minimum EUR 11 million.
Propose
Set a condition (if … then)
Refuse politely
Concede (give something)
Ask for clarification
Summarise and confirm
Ex 6.2Phrases for the table7 minFRAMEWORK · D3

A table to keep, and four risky sentences to replace. Then use both in the role-play.

FunctionUseful phrasesCareful
ProposeWe would like to propose… · Our proposal is… · Would you consider…?"Would" is softer than "will": use it to open.
ConditionIf you… we will… · We could accept that, provided… · On condition that…"If" starts a trade. Avoid "provided that": it is ambiguous in a contract (Day 4).
Refuse politelyI am afraid we cannot… · That is difficult for us because… · We would find it hard to accept…Give a reason. A refusal without a reason sounds like a wall.
ConcedeWe are prepared to move on… · We could be flexible on…Never concede without asking for something in return.
ClarifyCould you explain…? · What do you mean by…? · Do you mean…?Ask before you answer: it gives you time.
SummariseSo, to confirm… · Let me check I have understood… · We have agreed that…Summarise numbers aloud, then confirm them in writing “subject to contract”: nothing is agreed until the signed document exists.
Protect yourselfFor discussion purposes only · Subject to contract · Nothing in this email creates or amends any binding obligationNever write “we agree”, “accepted” or “final position” unless you mean to be bound.
TEACHER NOTE

Spoken and written. In the room: would, could, if. In the contract: must (duty), must not (ban), may (right), will (a future step of a procedure, such as “a Call-Off will become effective when both sign”). A negotiator who says "we shall pay" has made a promise; the same words in a contract may mean three things (Day 1).

Email-safe wording · replace the risky sentence

Risky sentenceSafer replacement
“We accept unlimited responsibility.”
“Go ahead; we are fully aligned.”
“We will cover all consequences.”
“The cap is agreed.”
Why is “Go ahead; we are fully aligned” risky in a project that runs on Call-Offs?
✗ Not quite. Look again.
✗ It is an everyday word; the risk is the message.
✗ Emails can create or evidence commitments.
✓ D3 clause 4: a quotation, purchase order or routine email does not by itself create a Call-Off, and the Contractor must not start chargeable work without an effective Call-Off or a signed early-work authorisation. A careless email invites an argument anyway (verify under Italian law).

What D3 says today (the draft on the table)

16.1 Each Party's aggregate ordinary liability… is capped at: for each Call-Off, 100% of the Contract Price of that Call-Off, subject to a minimum of EUR 10,000,000.

15 Delay damages apply only to milestones, rates and caps expressly identified in a Call-Off… they are the sole monetary remedy for the relevant milestone delay. Call-Off No. 1 (Schedule 1): Final Acceptance EUR 30,000 per day, cap EUR 2,520,000; aggregate cap EUR 4,200,000.

🟦 Card · GER (open if you are GER)
IssueYour openingYour limit

🟧 Card · Meridian (open if you are Meridian)
IssueYour openingYour limit

TEACHER NOTE · the overlap

Both limits overlap: cap EUR 11 to 12 million at 100%; delay damages EUR 25,000 per day and a total cap of 10% of the price; notice 90 days. Participants who reveal their limit lose leverage. The deal exists: the lesson is the language of reaching it.

Pairs of three? A third participant is the observer and listens for: which function each sentence performs (Ex 6.1) and whether any concession was made without asking for something in return.

The figures are fiction. D3 in the file says 100% and EUR 10,000,000 (16.1), 60 days (20), and for Final Acceptance EUR 30,000 per day with an aggregate cap of EUR 4,200,000 (Schedule 1); nothing of the role-play changes the document.

Meeting notes, GER and Meridian, 22 October (role-play)
1. Cap: roughly 100% of the Call-Off price, with a minimum of EUR 11,000,000 or so. Both Parties are covered.
